utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all. Registrar, kindly call the case in today's hearing, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is case number IT-98-32/1-A, the Prosecutor versus Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to know whether Mr. Milan Lukic and Mr. Sredoje Lukic can hear and follow the proceedings in a language they understand. THE APPELLANT M. LUKIC: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, yes. I'm Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Milan Lukic. And what about Mr. Sredoje Lukic, please. THE APPELLANT S. LUKIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Sredoje Lukic. May I have the appearances now, please, starting off with Mr. Milan Lukic's counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Counsel Tomislav Visnjic and Dan Ivetic appearing for Milan Lukic, together with Mrs. Marie O'Leary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Let me now turn to Mr. Sredoje Lukic's counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Sredoje Lukic, myself, Djuro Cepic, as Defence counsel; appearing with me at this bench, on my left-hand side, Professor Knoops as our legal consultant; on my right-hand side, Mr. Jens Dieckmann as co-counsel; and behind me, in your view from right to left, Ms. Sabine Schulz, Mr. Jacob Nuebel, and Ms. Marritta van Wandenberg as our legal assistants. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Let me now turn to the representatives of the OTP, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Peter Kremer appearing on behalf of the Prosecution assisted today and tomorrow by Matthew Gillett, who is on my right; Matthias Schuster; and Virginie Monchy; Colin Nawrot is assisting us as our case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Appeals Chamber is sitting today to hear the parties' submissions raised as part of the appeals lodged by Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, and the OTP against the judgement issued on 20th of July, 2009, by the Trial Chamber III. Before I give the floor to the parties, let me give you the procedural background and sum up the grounds of appeal raised in this case. I shall also tell you how we are going to proceed during these two days of hearing. This case concerns Mr. Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic, cousins and originating from Rujiste, a village close to Visegrad, and it relates to the events that unfolded between June 1992 and October 1994 in Visegrad. Milan Lukic lived at the time with his parents in a house located on Pionirska Street in Visegrad. Sredoje Lukic, on the other hand, was during these events a policeman assigned to the Visegrad police station. In its judgement, Trial Chamber III entered a finding of guilt for Milan Lukic on 19 out of the 21 charges against him under Article 7(1) of the Statute, including the crimes of persecution, extermination, murder, inhumane acts as crimes against humanity, as well as murder and cruel treatment as a violation of the laws or customs of war. He faces a term of life imprisonment. Sredoje Lukic was convicted to a single 30 years' imprisonment sentence for seven out of the 13 charges against him, including the crimes of persecution, murder, and inhumane acts as crimes against humanity and murder and cruel treatment as a violation of the laws or customs of war. Milan Lukic appealed against the Trial Chamber's judgement on the 19th of August, 2009, and submits eight grounds of appeal. Under his first ground of appeal, Milan Lukic submits that the Trial Chamber committed an error of law and of fact when it entered a finding of guilt as regards the events that took place on June the 7th, 1992, along the Drina River which led to seven Muslim civilian victims. Under his second ground of appeal, Milan Lukic raises errors of law and fact relating to his guilt for the murder of seven civilians in the Varda factory around the 10th of June, 1992. Under his third ground of appeal, he submits that errors of law and fact were committed with regard to his guilt for the crimes committed in the house on Pionirska Street where 59 Muslim civilians were burnt alive. He also avers that errors were committed in the assessment of his alibi. Under his fourth ground of appeal, he submits that the Trial Chamber committed an error of law and of fact when it concluded that he had participated in the events where 60 Muslim civilians were burnt alive in a house in Bikavac. Under his fifth ground of appeal, Milan Lukic challenges the findings of the Trial Chamber in respect of his shooting of a Muslim civilian Hajra Koric. Under his sixth ground of appeal, he invokes errors of law and fact regarding the conclusion that he had participated in the inhumane treatment of Muslim civilians detained in the Uzamnica camp. Under his seventh ground of appeal, he invokes a number of violations of his right to a fair trial. Under his eighth and last ground of appeal, Milan Lukic submits that errors of law and fact were committed as regards his sentence. On the other hand, Sredoje Lukic appealed the Trial Chamber judgement of the 19th of August, 2009. In support of his application to overturn the judgement, Sredoje Lukic submits five grounds of appeal. In his -- under his grounds of appeal one to seven, Sredoje Lukic submits errors of law and errors of fact against his guilt due to the role he played in the events that took place on the Pionirska Street around the 10th of June, 1992. He invokes, inter alia, errors in the assessment of the Prosecution evidence and Defence evidence with regard to his alibi as well as errors committed relating to the legal findings in respect of the mens rea and actus reus elements of the crimes he is charged with. Under grounds of appeal eight to ten, Sredoje Lukic submits errors of law and of fact as regards his responsibility and his role in the inhumane treatment inflicted on Muslim civilians detained in the Uzamnica camp. Under his 11th and 12th ground of appeal, he invokes errors of law and of fact regarding his conviction for the crime of persecution and the acts he committed during the events on the Pionirska Street and in the Uzamnica camp. As part of his 13th ground of appeal, he alleges that the Trial Chamber misapplied the principle of in dubio pro reo. Under his 14th ground of appeal, he invokes errors of law as regards the in-court identification procedure. Under his 15th ground of appeal, he submits errors of law and of fact against the sentence imposed on him by the Trial Chamber. On the other hand, the Prosecutor submits two grounds of appeal regarding Sredoje Lukic's conviction. Under his -- its first ground of appeal, the Prosecutor alleges an error of law committed by the Trial Chamber when it did not convict Sredoje Lukic for the crime of extermination due to his involvement in the crimes committed on Pionirska Street. Under its second ground of appeal, the Prosecutor alleges an error of law committed by the Trial Chamber for having omitted to convict Sredoje Lukic for the crime of persecution committed during the events in the Uzamnica camp. At this hearing counsel of both parties may decide to make their submissions regarding their subgrounds and grounds of appeal in the order they deem the most timely. I wish, however, to remind the parties have been asked to develop a number of questions that have been disclosed to them in the order aimed at preparing the hearing of the 6th of September, 2011. In accordance with Article 25 of the Statute, the arguments of the appellant must be restricted to the areas regarding a question of law which invalidates a decision and to errors of fact which have caused a miscarriage of justice. The appeals hearing is not a trial de novo and the appellant cannot merely repeat arguments already heard by the Trial Chamber. The appellant has, furthermore, the obligation to provide precise references to the elements in support of its submissions on appeal. The Appeals Chamber would very much appreciate it if the parties were to make their submissions in a clear, orderly, and concise fashion, avoiding any word-for-word submissions contained in their respective trial briefs. I would like to inform the parties that Judges may take the liberty at any time to put questions to the parties if necessary and may put their questions at the beginning or after each of their presentations. This hearing will unfold pursuant to the order -- Scheduling Order of the 8th of July, 2011. I would like now to ask Milan Lukic counsel to make their submissions. Let me remind you that you have one hour and 15 minutes. I now turn to you, Milan Lukic's counsel, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We have divided our submissions into two parts. In the first part, I will be speaking about certain omissions made by the Trial Chamber regarding identification evidence, identification of the appellant; and at the end, Mr. Dan Ivetic will address the questions you have posed in your 6 September order. Your Honours, I begin with the hopefully uncontentious observation that in times of crisis and conflict, certain individuals become infamous by reputation, rumours spread like wildfire, legends are born. Myths are created by elements of truth, by falsity, and by exaggeration. A face is perceived when it could not in reality have been present. The Trial Chambers of this Tribunal face the difficult task of sifting through evidence of horrendous crimes to establish beyond reasonable doubt what happened and who is responsible. Your Honours, the experience of criminal justice systems around the world shows that claims of identification and recognition are fertile ground for miscarriages of justice. This is well-known ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is well-known and so the law has developed to address obvious risks. Objective identification procedures are used, such as identification parades or independently vetted photo-boards. The first time a witness is interviewed by the police or a prosecuting authority, interviews are recorded to ensure that words are not put into a witness's mouth. A witness is asked for detailed descriptions of a perpetrator. If the witness thought that they recognised the perpetrator, the basis for the recognition is established. When the case finally comes to court, legal principles govern the assessment of any identification evidence. Why? Because even at that stage the risk exists of a miscarriage of justice. The trier of fact must methodically scrutinise the evidence against the right legal standards. [In English] Yes, thank you. [Interpretation] The Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal has summarised the standards in successive cases, for example, Kupreskic, Kvocka, and Limaj, among others. These standards were recently confirmed by the Appeals Chamber in Haradinaj. The relevant parts of those authorities set out the approach that a Trial Chamber should take to identification evidence. The Trial Chamber in this case did not direct itself to the binding standards that should have guided its assessment of the identification evidence before it. In the section of the trial judgement where the Trial Chamber set out the law around evidentiary matters, there is no mention of the relevant authorities. That's 1D section of the trial judgement. Neither did the Trial Chamber direct itself to or apply the relevant authorities when reviewing the evidence in relation to the six crime sites. Why is this important? What impact did it have on the judgement? After all, as the Prosecution observes, the Presiding Judge had noted during the course of the trial that identification was an essential issue in the case. Moreover, as the Prosecution points out, the Trial Chamber did consider some of the identification evidence in relation to each crime site. Your Honours, the point is this: We do not deny that at times the Trial Chamber considered the types of factors one would expect it to consider had it indeed directed itself to the relevant authorities. But, Your Honours, that is not enough. We say that the Trial Chamber's failure to direct itself to the relevant law meant that it did not have the correct standards in mind when considering the evidence identifying perpetrators in this case. That the Trial Chamber touched upon some of the relevant considerations by chance does not mean that it scrutinised those factors with sufficient rigour, nor does it change the fact that it missed other relevant considerations entirely. Of particular concern, Your Honours, is the Trial Chamber's approach to claims by certain witnesses that they were able to recognise Milan Lukic as a perpetrator. In particular, the Trial Chamber accepted claims of recognition, in many instances made years later, without scrupulously examining the basis for claimed recognition or considering the possibility that a claim of recognition was genuinely or otherwise mistaken. The Trial Chamber even held that witnesses recognised Milan Lukic when the Prosecution had conceded in its closing brief that there was an insufficient basis for recognition. The most glaring example of this is Witness VG-13, perhaps the most important Prosecution witness in relation to the Pionirska Street fire and the only witness who claimed that they saw Milan Lukic place the explosive device into the room. Your Honours, at paragraph 157 of its closing brief, the Prosecution said that the evidence did not clearly establish that VG-13 could be described as a recognition witness. However, the Trial Chamber, no doubt influenced by its failure to direct itself to the correct legal standards, held that VG-13 had solid prior knowledge of Milan Lukic, such that she recognised him. That's in paragraph 612 of the trial judgement. This witness also claimed to recognise Mitar Vasiljevic as being present during the Pionirska fire, a point to which I will turn later in due course. The Prosecution says that the Tribunal jurisprudence has adopted a common-sense proposition, namely, that recognition evidence is generally more reliable than identification evidence. We say that this does not accurately reflect the jurisprudence and is a dangerous submission. In our brief, we explain how recognition evidence is not necessarily more reliable than identification evidence. We have all experienced that sense of thinking we have recognised an old acquaintance when it turns out to be somebody completely different. Your Honours, with your leave, we will make brief submissions on the impact of the Trial Chamber's error in relation to each specific crime site. Before doing so, however - and again with your permission - I would like to address you on two issues. The first issue is the impact of the repeated in-court identifications of Milan Lukic by Prosecution witnesses during the trial. We say that this is relevant to every single crime site. The second issue is the Trial Chamber's treatment of the evidence surrounding the alleged presence of Mitar Vasiljevic in Visegrad on key dates. This is relevant to the Pionirska Street fire and also the Bikavac incident. Concerning the identity of the accused in the courtroom, the identification of the accused in the courtroom, I would like to present four points. The first point is to emphasise the prejudice made to the appellant by in-court identifications. It affected negatively the consideration of the Trial Chamber of the evidence given by witnesses who claimed to recognise Milan Lukic in the courtroom. Your Honours, in the recent Haradinaj case, the Appeals Chamber recognised that even when individual decisions might have normally been within the scope of the Trial Chamber's discretion, the context of a trial can require the Trial Chamber to proactively focus on ensuring the fairness of the proceedings. The approach of the Appeals Chamber in Haradinaj was to review the Trial Chamber's decisions cumulatively rather than individually. Your Honours, in our respectful submission, you should adopt the same approach when addressing the impact of in-court identifications in this case. Even if an individual in-court identification was permissible, the Appeals Chamber should consider the impact of the repeated in-court identifications on the judgement. The circumstances of this case were not normal. The case against Milan Lukic turned almost exclusively upon the evidence of eye-witnesses being asked detailed questions about what they saw some 16 years ago. For example, in relation to the Pionirska Street fire, whether VG-13 was able to identify Milan Lukic as the person who opened the door and threw an explosive device inside when it was night-time and there was no electricity inside the room. We say that where identity is in dispute and the case hinges upon the ability of witnesses to accurately identify the accused as a perpetrator - especially after the passage of so many years - it unduly prejudices any defendant to ask a witness to identify the perpetrator for the first time in court. We say that the Prosecution should have performed a fair out-of-court identification procedure. We say that the approach adopted in this case denied Milan Lukic the fundamental protection offered by more objective identification procedures. Your Honours, if the Prosecution was so certain on the reliability of its identification evidence, why did it not systematically use a fair out-of-court procedure? Why did it not follow the procedures set out in the Tribunal's manual of developed practices? It would have nothing to lose, but the fairness of these proceedings had everything to gain. The repeated in-court identifications of the appellant in court resulted in at least two kinds of prejudice to these proceedings. Firstly, we question the ability of any trier of fact to ignore a witness identification of the accused in the dock as the perpetrator they say they saw commit a horrendous crime against them or others. The Prosecution says that in general, although not always, the Trial Chamber relied upon evidence of prior knowledge and recognition and not the in-court identifications. We say that the language of the Trial Chamber -- trial judgement defies what actually happened. For example, in relation to the Bikavac fire, two of three of the Prosecution's main witnesses identified Milan Lukic in court, VG-58 and VG-115. The Trial Chamber relied upon these witnesses' supposed recognition of Milan Lukic, despite holding that neither witness had stood up to cross-examination. In one part of the judgement the Trial Chamber held that Witness VG-58 was evasive and indeed her first witness statement contained no reference to Milan Lukic in relation to the Bikavac incident. In another part of the judgement, the Trial Chamber held that Witness VG-115 did not stand up well under cross-examination. You can find more details of this in our appeals submission 101 and 102 paragraphs and other paragraphs as well. Yet, despite these findings the Trial Chamber held that Milan Lukic had been identified by credible and reliable witnesses. We say that this does not stack up and that the obvious factor behind this shift is that when asked if they could identify who they saw was the perpetrator, they pointed to Milan Lukic sitting in the dock. Secondly, the practice of in-court identification prejudices the witnesses' own evidence. By being asked to pick out the accused in the courtroom, it is artificially reinforced in their mind that it was the accused who they saw commit a crime. For example, in relation to the Pionirska Street fire, Witness VG-13 was one of numerous witnesses who identified Milan Lukic in court, claiming that they could recognise him. We say that VG-13's evidence changed significantly after picking Milan Lukic out in court. Before that, there was little hard evidence of prior knowledge, such that the Defence could test her claim to recognise Milan Lukic rather than simply implicate him because he was notorious. However, after identifying him in court the witness began to allege all manner of prior knowledge. The Trial Chamber proceeded to find that Witness VG-13 had solid prior knowledge of Milan Lukic. Your Honours, the Prosecution had conceded at trial - and I quote from the Prosecution's closing brief - VG-13 had heard of Milan Lukic prior to that day, but it was on that day she recalls seeing him for the first time. That's paragraph 156 of the Prosecution closing brief. There it is, Your Honours. The Prosecution itself could see that rumour and myth played a factor in VG-13 placing Milan Lukic on Pionirska Street on the 14th of June, 1992. We say that VG-13's claim to recognise Milan Lukic was polluted by her being allowed to identify him in court. The Prosecution conceded as much at trial, albeit it now tries an inelegant U-turn on appeal. We would also note, Your Honours, that the Prosecution points to the evidence VG-13 gave under cross-examination as showing that she was a recognition witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this demonstrates that she had not been established as a recognition witness at the point in the court identification was attempted. Second point, in-court identification by recognition witnesses. The submission that the Trial Chamber correctly allowed in-court identification by recognition witnesses is our second point. Our preliminary observation is that this is not a fact what happened in trial. There is no clear demarcation between identification witnesses on the one hand and recognition witnesses on the other hand, such that different legal standards can apply to one compared to the other. The reality, as the Office of the Prosecutor conceded in the Tadic case, is that there is often a grey area when recognition is hazy or uncertain and hotly disputed. The Trial Chamber sought to distinguish the Limaj appeal judgement, the Kunarac appeal judgement, and the Kamuhanda appeal judgement at the ICTR and contends that while in-court identifications should be discouraged in relation to identification witnesses, there is no problem when they are conducted by recognition witnesses. We say that the Trial Chamber misstated the law, in the international law, when it said that such cases should be distinguished. For our second point is that the jurisprudence of this Tribunal did not allow for weight to be placed upon in-court identifications by recognition witnesses. Your Honours, our third point in relation to in-court identification is to address the Prosecution's submission that the Trial Chamber did not actually place any probative weight on them, save in relation one of the six crime sites, the Uzamnica detention camp. The Prosecution conceded that the Trial Chamber did place probative weight on the in-court identification of two witnesses to beatings in the Uzamnica detention camp. These are Witnesses Dervisevic and Berberovic, and the relevant paragraph of the judgement is 828. We say that the key point is that the Trial Chamber considered that it had to put weight on these in-court supposed recognitions of Milan Lukic, because otherwise there was insufficient evidence that these witnesses were in fact able to identify Milan Lukic as the perpetrator. Following the Prosecution's logic, there was insufficient evidence of prior knowledge and identifying information provided by these witnesses. Generic descriptions of physical characteristics that could fit almost anyone are insufficient. In relation to Berberovic and Dervisevic's descriptions of Lukic's background, this was their evidence many years after the events. It was not what they had said at the time. Can we dwell briefly on the Trial Chamber's reasoning here. The Trial Chamber held that Berberovic and Dervisevic were recognition witnesses, but Berberovic's evidence was that he learned that the assailant was called Milan Lukic from Dervisevic, but Berberovic also testified that Dervisevic also had problems with his eyesight such that he could not see properly. Berberovic also said that another individual, the elusive watchman Muratagic told him that this man was Milan Lukic. The Defence was not able to cross-examine this individual as to whether he really did tell Berberovic that or whether he really was able to recognise Lukic. The Trial Chamber considered it had to rely upon these in-court identifications on Milan Lukic because the other evidence against him was so weak. We ask that the Appeals Chamber rule that no weight should have been placed on these court identifications. It inexorably follows that the finding that Berberovic and Dervisevic were able to recognise Milan Lukic must be overturned. Fourth and last point we want to address in relation to in-court identifications is this. We say that the Trial Chamber's error is demonstrated by its treatment of the failure of its star witness to the Bikavac fire, Zehra Turjacanin, to be able to identify Milan Lukic in court. At paragraph 724 of the Trial Chamber's judgement, the Trial Chamber simply said that it placed little weight on her inability to pick Milan Lukic out in court. It gave no explanation as to how or why it could reach such a conclusion. We say that the Trial Chamber erred in law and in fact. To be clear, our submission is --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: There is a problem. [Interpretation] The Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber -- I would like to clarify that Defence is not claiming that the failure of a witness to recognise a defendant in the court must necessarily mean that all of their identification evidence is excluded. For example, in Limaj, the Appeals Chamber referred to the approach in Kvocka as meaning that a failure to identify an accused can simply be a reason for declining to rely on the evidence of a witness. We concede that, yes, it can be a reason, but it must be considered carefully and explained. In our case, the Trial Chamber simply didn't grasp this nettle. It didn't explain how it could ignore Zehra Turjacanin's inability to identify Milan Lukic in court. We are left to scratch our heads. We say the Trial Chamber merely accepted Zehra Turjacanin's claim to recognise Milan Lukic and failed to properly deal with the difficulties with this witness's evidence. These submissions are outlined in paragraphs 245 to 257 of our appeal brief and paragraph 98 of our reply brief. Your Honours, this concludes my submissions in relation to the conduct of in-court identifications. I would propose that we move next on the issue I identify which is the Trial Chamber's treatment of the evidence surrounding the alleged presence of Mitar Vasiljevic in Visegrad on June the 14th, 1992. This is relevant primarily to the Pionirska Street fire but also has implications for the Bikavac incident. Your Honours, before we move to the error made by the Trial Chamber, it may assist you if I begin by making clear why we say the presence or absence of Mitar Vasiljevic is relevant to Milan Lukic. Whether or not Mitar Vasiljevic was present on Pionirska Street split the Trial Chamber. The majority found that Vasiljevic was present, whereas Judge Robinson dissented and found that Vasiljevic could not have been there, just like the Trial Chamber had in Vasiljevic's own case. If a witness is demonstrably mistaken, even lying with respect to the presence of Mitar Vasiljevic, that must be considered with respect to the credibility of their claim that they were able to identify Milan Lukic as being there alongside with Vasiljevic. The point is reinforced because Vasiljevic was the more well-known of the two. He was the waiter who everybody knew. The majority Trial Chamber relied on the evidence of VG-13, VG-37, VG-78, and VG-101 and held that those witnesses were credible such as to establish the presence of Mitar Vasiljevic was present on Pionirska Street. The Trial Chamber relied upon those same witnesses to establish the presence of Milan Lukic at key points. For example, VG-13 said that it was Mitar Vasiljevic together with Milan Lukic who closed the door of the Adem Omeragic's house on Pionirska Street as the incendiary device was thrown inside. VG-13 said that when they were inside Adem Omeragic's house, Mitar Vasiljevic shone a torch up at the windows looking for anyone trying to escape while Milan Lukic fired shots. Your Honours, this relates to paragraphs 163 and 164 of our appeal brief. This witness claimed to have been able to recognise both Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic. If a witness is obviously mistaken as to the presence of one, that remains as to the presence of the other. Therefore, if you find that the Trial Chamber erred in law and fact as to the presence of Mitar Vasiljevic, you must consider its impact on the Trial Chamber's finding as to the presence of Milan Lukic. We have elaborated this in our subground 3(E) of our appeal brief. Your Honours, this concludes the Defence submissions with regard to the importance of Vasiljevic's presence during an incendiary event at Adem Omeragic's house in Pionirska Street. And now we would like to address you on the impact of the Trial Chamber's failure to consider the binding standards in relation to each of the six crime sites. I would like to start with the Drina River incident. Your Honours, there were four witnesses to the shooting on the banks of the Drina River on 7 June 1992. They were VG-14 and VG-32 who were survivors. Mitar Vasiljevic was one of the shooters and was convicted separately for his part. VG-73 witnessed events from the other side of the river. The Trial Chamber did not rely upon his evidence as being capable of identifying Milan Lukic, and so we do not address this witness's evidence at all. Dealing firstly with Mitar Vasiljevic, Witnesses VG-14 and VG-32 testified against him in his own trial. We say in subground 1(F) of our appeal brief that having heard their evidence, Vasiljevic's evidence was bound to be what he thought would be most likely to get him off the hook. Those witnesses thought that they had seen Mitar Vasiljevic with Milan Lukic. Vasiljevic thought that there was a good chance that he would be convicted. The incentive was there for him to corroborate aspects of their evidence while seeking to minimise his own involvement. Knowing that Milan Lukic had not been arrested and thinking he never would be, Vasiljevic implicated the other person that VG-14 and VG-32 had said was there and sought to shift the blame onto that second person. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber failed to examine this likelihood. Its reliance on the evidence of VG-14 as corroborating Vasiljevic's story is insufficient. Vasiljevic's incentive was to corroborate VG-14's story. VG-14 claimed that he recognised Milan Lukic even though he hadn't seen him since they were 16 in 1984. There is no direction in the trial judgement to the danger of mistaken recognition in such circumstances. In VG-14's first statement after the shootings, which was in 1998, six years after the incident, he describes Milan Lukic as somebody who has a distinctively large birthmark on the right side cheek. Your Honours, the Prosecution tries to diminish this aspect of VG-14's evidence by suggesting that VG-14 referred to a birthmark or a mole. But in the first statement we have, albeit six years after the crime, his words are that the birthmark was distinctive and large. The Prosecution says that the Chamber relied on VG-14's demeanour. We say that even a confident and a convincing witness can be mistaken and misleading. The failure of the Trial Chamber to direct itself to such possibilities in the treacherous field of identification evidence results in miscarriages of justice. VG-32 did not know Milan Lukic either, as we explain in paragraphs 46 through 49 of our appeal brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The proper course for the Prosecution would have been to perform objective out-of-court identification procedures. The Trial Chamber should have set out the relevant legal principles and applied them. Neither of these things happened. Let us turn to the Varda factory incident. The Trial Chamber relied primarily on the evidence of Witness VG-42. Your Honours, the primary witness in this case identified, or rather, claimed that she was able to identify Milan Lukic from at least 50 metres, someone who on her own evidence had last seen Lukic when he was a child. Your Honours, we say that the Trial Chamber utterly failed to give the necessary scrutiny to such a claim. We say that this witness exaggerated what she was able to see as the years had gone by. Of particular importance, Your Honours, is VG-42's first witness statement given in 1993. In that statement she doesn't identify Milan Lukic as the perpetrator of that crime, albeit, Your Honours, she does associate him with crimes around Visegrad. It was only in 1998 that this witness identified Milan Lukic for specified crimes including the disappearance of her husband. The trial judgement fails to properly scrutinise the likelihood that VG-42 misidentified the shooter because of the distance involved. Similarly with VG-24, the Trial Chamber failed to consider the possibility of mistaken recognition. VG-24 had misidentified Milan Lukic on at least two occasions. The Trial Chamber erred by simply diminishing these misidentifications. Overall, there was no evidence that Milan Lukic was indeed the shooter. The standard of proof in relation to this crime site was far short of that which an international criminal tribunal should accept. With regard to the Pionirska Street incident we would like to say the following. The criteria witness of the fire at Adem Omeragic's house on Pionirska Street were VG-13, VG-78, and VG-101. Each of these witnesses claimed that Mitar Vasiljevic was present and we have made submissions on this point already. Witness VG-13 was not a recognition witness and the Prosecution conceded as much as trial. On appeal the Prosecution reverses its position and contends that there was ample opportunity for VG-13 to recognise Milan Lukic. Your Honours, the Prosecution must be held to its initial position and the position was that VG-13 did not know Milan Lukic but implicated him subsequently. The Prosecution had no other evidence that Milan Lukic had started the fire, and just as the Trial Chamber in the Vasiljevic case held that the stress of the situation undermined VG-13's identification of Mitar Vasiljevic, the Trial Chamber should have made the analogous conclusion in this case. Witnesses VG-78 and VG-101 are sisters. They claim that they went to school with Milan Lukic some ten years before the Pionirska Street incident. The Trial Chamber failed to scrutinise such a weak basis as a claim for recognition. Your Honours, you should compare the scrutiny that the Vasiljevic Trial Chamber gave to the evidence of these witnesses compared to the approach of the Trial Chamber in this case. The Vasiljevic Trial Chamber rejected the evidence of these witnesses as being unreliable because it had scrutinised them to a greater degree, having set out the factors it would consider in paragraph 16 of that judgement. In relation to the question of lighting, the Trial Chamber completely failed to consider the difficulties encountered when attempting to identify someone at night. The Prosecution says that there were various light sources that made it possible to see the perpetrators, and we say that this just wasn't enough. We have no clear indication that the Trial Chamber scrutinised the level of lighting involved and what it would have looked like to the witnesses involved. Simply pointing to the odd source of light on the evening of the 14th of June, 1992, as the Prosecution seeks to do, is insufficient. The key witnesses in relation to Bikavac are Zehra Turjacanin, VG-58, and VG-115. The Trial Chamber held that Milan Lukic's presence was established by credible and reliable witnesses. We have already addressed you in relation to Zehra Turjacanin's testimony already. She could not have recognised Milan Lukic because she didn't know him. Rather, she implicated Milan Lukic and his group on the basis of apparent notoriety. We note that she also implicated Mitar Vasiljevic in the Bikavac fire, but, as we know, Mitar Vasiljevic had broken his leg badly only a week beforehand and could not feasibly have been present. Indeed, the Office of the Prosecutor withdrew all charges against Vasiljevic in relation to Bikavac. In relation to Witnesses VG-58 and VG-115, the Trial Chamber held that they were evasive, they did not stand up well under cross-examination, yet inexplicably these clear findings were not considered in the final analysis. Had the Trial Chamber considered the proper legal standards and applied them consistently throughout the trial judgement, it would have been bound to reject the evidence of these witnesses. The fundamental inconsistencies in the accounts of these witnesses, which the Trial Chamber itself recognised, necessitated the rejection of their evidence. Your Honours, we criticise in particular paragraph 718 of the trial judgement. It is a short paragraph, only two sentences long, but we say that the two sentences contradict each other. No reasoning was given as to how the Trial Chamber could rely on the evidence of these witnesses in the face of its finding that they were evasive and undermined by cross-examination. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber's consideration and assessment of the evidence surrounding the killing of Hajra Koric was inadequate. Two witnesses gave evidence about the killing of Hajra Koric, VG-35 and CW-2. VG-35 alleged that she recognised Milan Lukic because he had raped her, but, Your Honours, VG-35's description of the rapist did not match Milan Lukic. Her first statement described a man with blue eyes and birthmarks or moles all over his body. Your Honours, how is it simply possible for a Trial Chamber properly directed to the relevant standards to ignore such evidence? Similarly, in relation to Witness CW-2, this witness first described the assailant as having blond hair. The Trial Chamber failed to direct itself to the importance of witnesses' initial accounts of the events before they've had a chance to change as the years go by. Moreover, in her 2008 statement this witness suggests that some other Chetnik fired the first shot, that's 1D228. Moreover, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber could not reject these issues saying that the witnesses were not undermined in cross-examination. It had to explain how it could possibly accept such fundamentally contradictory evidence from the same witnesses. Concerning the impact of identification regarding Uzamnica events, we have already made submissions in subgrounds 6(A), 6(B), and 6(C) of our appeal. I would now like to move to a brief conclusion. Your Honours, Milan Lukic and others were notorious in Visegrad in 1992 because they had fought in the war and killed many Bosnians in combat. There were also numerous other allegations flying around, as there are in all conflicts. Most of these accusations remained untried and untested. In any event, the stories about Milan Lukic snowballed, fuelled by the fears of an escalating ethnic conflict. But this does not lessen the burden of this Tribunal to ensure that the necessary standard of proof is applied equally in all cases and to ensure that the right people are held responsible for the right atrocity. In the trial of Milan Lukic, the Prosecution failed to follow its own developed practices and the Trial Chamber failed to apply the most basic legal principles. Investigations were manifestly inadequate. With all due respect, we say that the Trial Chamber in this case erred and that it is high time to put these errors right. We say as difficult as a decision of this kind might be for Your Honours, Milan Lukic's conviction simply cannot stand. Only in that way will this Tribunal fulfil its duty. Now I would like to give the floor to my colleague, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. At this time I would like to briefly illuminate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to draw your attention, Mr. Ivetic, to the fact that you are left with 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My comments should only take ten. I would like to briefly illuminate our submissions in regards to subgrounds 3(I) and 4(H) of our appeal and the question posed if each of these events qualifies as extermination. As a preliminary matter, I would note that while we additionally believe that the Trial Chamber erred in convicting Milan Lukic for killings at Pionirska and Bikavac, our further arguments in this regard are set forth in the remainder of our third and fourth grounds of appeal. When it comes to extermination, we believe that the Trial Chamber misapplied the appropriate legal standard. We respectfully submit that the majority watered down the threshold required for the crime of extermination. The distinguishing legal element of extermination that sets it apart from the crime of murder is its massiveness. Under the decisional authority, this element of massiveness has been referred to as mass killings, that was in the Blagojevic trial judgement; "substantial killing," that was in the Semanza trial judgement; mass destruction, that was in Ntakirutimana, the appeals judgement, paragraph 516; or a killing on a massive or large scale, again the Blagojevic trial judgement; or as the Vasiljevic trial judgement specified, a "vast scheme of collective murder."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will try to slow down. Therefore, Your Honours, massiveness refers to the number of victims, not their character. We believe that in regards to Pionirska and Bikavac, the majority erred in its characterisation of the incidents as extermination. For Pionirska the majority relied upon the type of victims, the area they came from, and the manner in which the fire was prepared. That's from paragraph 945 of the trial judgement. In regard to Bikavac, the majority relied on the manner in which the house was prepared, the manner the victims were herded into the house, and the number and type of victims, specifically their vulnerability. That's paragraph 949 of the trial judgement. But, Your Honours, in each instance the Trial Chamber noted that the victims numbered approximately 60 persons. In finding this extermination, the majority approach runs contrary to the history of extermination under the law. Historically, extermination originated at Nuremberg. Since the IMT statute did not contain a clause for genocide, extermination was used to prosecute individuals. The original elements of extermination were defined as, first, a great pattern or plan of racial persecution; and second, specific conduct of the defendant in furtherance of that plan. Now, while the Nuremberg Tribunal recognised that none of the accused directly perpetrated the crimes, they were involved in the creation of "nationwide organised systems of cruelty and injustice." This, we submit, was in essence the origin of the expression of massiveness. As footnote 587 of the Vasiljevic trial judgement points out, the lowest figure from these World War II cases wherein extermination was applied was for a total of 733 killings. Both the ICTY and ICTR have ensured that the element of massiveness is maintained at a high level in their rulings aggregating multiple incidents, that was Akayesu, Stakic, Krstic; holding that the killings must be of such a scale to be prohibitive to identify victims with specificity, Ntakirutimana appeals judgement; and holding that massiveness is tied to the chapeau elements for humanity, also from Ntakirutimana. The jurisprudence has found only extermination for cases where the accused participated in an overarching JCE covering a wide area and thousands of victims. It has never been reduced to a situation smaller than a municipality except for now, in this trial judgement. I urge Your Honours to look at paragraph 222 of our appeal brief which sets out a table of the previous extermination cases in the ICTY and the ICTR and the number of victims in each. None of those are close to the instant case where 60 persons was deemed to qualify for massiveness. I note that the Prosecution in its brief has referred to the Krajisnik convictions for extermination at Pionirska and Bikavac, but I must point out that the Krajisnik Appeals Chamber reversed the extermination conviction, although it did not address whether the threshold had been met in those instances. Just as in the Vasiljevic trial judgement, where Vasiljevic was acquitted of extermination on other grounds, the Chamber did not assess whether these two incidents constituted extermination. Your Honours, we are asking you today to answer this unsettled question of law if the two 60-person groups at issue constitute killings on a scale sufficient to meet the high massiveness threshold of extermination, especially in this case where there is not a JCE. We believe that the Appeals Chamber should be guided by the Martic trial judgement, where the accused was found not guilty of extermination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ivetic, even if it is quite late, there has been some delay in our hearing today, which of course was involuntary and beyond our control. So we have basically revised the schedule for the day and we are already applying this new schedule, which means that we have arranged the various speakers according to this new schedule for the day. Therefore, could you please take this on board. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I am aware of the schedule and I have arranged my comments accordingly. I am near the end. I have two more points to raise. We believe the Appeals Chamber should be guided by the Martic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A new agenda will be circulated to the parties during the break, just for your information. So all parties will receive this new schedule for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, we believe that the Appeals Chamber should be guided by the Martic trial judgement, where the accused was found not guilty of extermination on the basis of the deaths of 165 victims. We submit, Your Honour, that this is the only ICTY case that has dealt with a number of victims remotely similar, and yet still higher than the instant case and in that case they correctly found that extermination was not appropriate. And that as bad as the crimes were, they are only qualifiedly murder. Also, Your Honour, Your Honours, we would ask you to look at the 2008 ICTR trial judgement of Zigiranyirazo, where the Chamber found massiveness was satisfied by an incident where "hundreds and possibly over a thousand were killed, but the same Chamber deemed that "at least 10 to 20" persons killed at a roadblock in another incident was not sufficient to achieve massiveness or a conviction of extermination. And that is from paragraphs 434 to 439 of that judgement. Accordingly, Your Honours, we would respectfully ask for the convictions of extermination against Milan Lukic to be reversed and for this error by the majority to be corrected by the appropriate appellate relief. And I thank you for your time. If there are no questions, I believe that finishes the submission of the Milan Lukic Defence on appeal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. We are now going to have a break of 30 minutes, and the hearing shall resume at 11.30, half past 11.00. Court stands adjourned until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. I would like to invite the representatives of the OTP to present their submissions in response, but before doing so, before doing so, as I was saying, Judge Liu has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I have a question to ask the appellant counsel. I'm very much interested in the -- in your submission concerning the required number for the crime of extermination. I believe that there is some case law concerning this issue. In the Brdjanin case, the Trial Chamber said that: "While the extermination generally involves a large number of the victims, it may be constituted even where the number of the victims is limited." And on the Stakic case, the Trial Chamber said that: "The killing must have occurred on a vast scale in a concentrated place over a short period of time." And also in the Blagojevic case, the Trial Chamber said: "While some Trial Chambers have discussed whether the elements of the mass destruction includes a minimum number of victims, the Trial Chamber found that there's no such requirement. In the Trial Chamber's opinion, any such attempt to set a minimum number of the victims in the abstract will ultimately prove unhelpful. The element of massive scale must be assessed on a case-by-case basis in light of the proven criminal conduct and all relevant factors." I just want to know the counsel's comments on that jurisprudence in the ICTY Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's a very good question. We are not asking the Appeals Chamber to set a minimum threshold for the crime of extermination. The case law that Your Honour pointed out is clear that there is no minimum threshold for this crime, and I would also add the Ntakirutimana appeal judgement at paragraph 516, I believe, is one that also dealt with that, in addition to the authorities you discussed. What we are asking you to do is perform the case-by-case analysis that was called for in the Stakic appeals judgement at paragraph 260, to look at this particular case, to determine if the entire totality of the facts for each incident involving 60 persons is appropriate to meet the threshold of massiveness for extermination, such that a conviction would be supportable. The case we mentioned, the Martic trial judgement, in that case, Your Honour, the Court looked at the totality of the evidence to find that the incidents, 165 killings, whether considered alone or aggregated on a cumulative basis was not enough to amount to extermination. In particular, they focused on the crimes being committed in a limited time and limited area. In the appeals judgement in Brdjanin, on the other hand, extermination was found applicable, including for 68 persons in Brisevo, but under the totality of 1.669 persons killed in many incidents covering the entire ARK municipalities' territory. Also considered in light of the surrounding circumstances of the killings happening at that time. That was paragraph 472 of the appeals judgement. As the Appeals Chamber in Brdjanin rightly noted, the Brdjanin trial judgement considered all killings in the ARK territory as a whole rather than as individual incidents. They aggregated them together. In this case we submit that you must take into account that, unlike the others, there is no joint criminal enterprise, no overarching plan across a wide territory. Likewise, we submit, that this case is closer to the rationale in Martic than in -- to Brdjanin and we believe that extermination is not appropriate to describe these events, again under the totality of the facts on a case-by-case analysis for this case. Based upon the fact that the killings are said to have occurred over a limited time, a limited area, by limited persons, and with no JCE. I hope that will answer your question, Judge Liu. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that I will hear the view -- the point of view from the Prosecution on this subject in their submission later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, you will, Your Honour. Your Honours, in 1992 and 1993, Milan Lukic murdered, terrorised, and viciously beat numerous Bosnian Muslims in and around the small town of Visegrad. Having listened to the witnesses' harrowing accounts of these events and having weighed the evidence, the Trial Chamber properly convicted Milan Lukic for the crimes charged in the indictment. On appeal, Milan Lukic essentially submits that this was a case of mistaken identity. However, the Chamber heard compelling evidence placing him at each of the crime sites. The witnesses and victims that recognised him included his former schoolmates, his acquaintances, and other members of the small community that he came from. He fails to show that the Trial Chamber erred and that his appeal should be dismissed. In responding to Milan Lukic's submissions today, I will address, first, the law governing identification evidence and demonstrate why Milan Lukic has failed to show any error in the Trial Chamber's approach to identification. Second, I will address the key pieces of evidence supporting the Trial Chamber's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you kindly slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: -- conviction of Milan Lukic for the Pionirska Street fire and the Bikavac fire, focussing again on identification. And third, I will deal with the question on extermination and address the question that Judge Liu has just asked to my learned friend Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: You're kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Following my submissions, Ms. Monchy will address the Drina River and Varda factory killings and answer any questions the Chamber may have on the Koric murder. Finally, Mr. Schuster will deal with the conviction for the crimes committed in the Uzamnica camp. I will point out now that the Prosecution will not address the Milan Lukic submissions on proof of death that were made in his briefs, but rely on our Prosecution response brief in its responses to Milan Lukic's Rule 115 applications dealing with the subject. The same applies to his legal and factual submissions on alibi which have not been addressed today. And we are available should you have any questions on these subjects to answer questions. At the outset, it's important to recall that this was a very -- very much a case about people, about individual experiences. The people of Visegrad came forward to speak about the violence and killings inflicted by one of their neighbours. Many of them had been subject to brutal attacks or witnesses to brutal attacks. They were often traumatised by what they experienced or saw. The Trial Chamber was in a unique position to evaluate whether each of the witnesses was reliable and credible about the events that they saw, heard, and suffered through. As the ICTR Appeals Chamber stated in Nahimana at paragraph 949: "Trial Judges are in the best position to assess the credibility of a witness and the reliability of the evidence adduced." This Appeals Chamber should afford the Trial Chamber in this case the proper deference in these matters. The minor anomalies or inconsistencies that Milan Lukic raises on appeal were addressed by the Trial Chamber where relevant and are set out in its judgement. It was not required to address mere hypothetical possibilities without any basis in the evidence. It is only fair or rational possibilities arising from the evidence as a whole that need to be addressed, as Your Honours have stated in the Mrksic appeals judgement at paragraph 220. Milan Lukic raises none that warrant appellate intervention and you should not allow Milan Lukic to turn this case or this appeal into a trial de novo. Turning now to identification evidence. As I mentioned, this case essentially turned on the issue of identification and the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber adopted a careful approach to identification evidence. As Mr. Visnjic properly pointed out, very early in the proceedings Judge Robinson commented: "The essential issue in this case is identity." So the Trial Chamber was very well aware of the importance of identification in this trial. The Trial Chamber did not ignore the legal principles governing identification evidence, as Milan Lukic suggests, and although the judgement does not set out at length the guiding principles on identification evidence, as Milan Lukic submits is a requirement, the Trial Chamber referred to judgements containing the applicable jurisprudence. At paragraph 31 of its judgement, the Chamber referred to paragraph 9 [sic] of the Haradinaj trial judgement which sets out the guidance from the Kupreskic appeal judgement, which in Kupreskic stated: "The Appeals Chamber highlighted several factors to be considered when evaluating identification evidence, including identification by witnesses who only had a fleeting glance or an obstructed view of an accused; identification occurring in the dark; identification as a result of a traumatic event experienced by the witness; inconsistent or inaccurate testimony about the accused's physical characteristics at the time of the event; and a witness's delayed assertion of memory regarding an accused coupled with the clear possibility from the circumstances that the witness had been influenced by suggestions from others. When confronted with recognition evidence, rather than identification evidence stricto sensu, the Trial Chamber also took into account the possibility of bias, and the interval between the time the witness recognised the person and the time he had last seen him." That's the quote from paragraph -- from Kupreskic which is referred to in the Haradinaj judgement. And all of those factors are factors that were applicable to some or all of the evidence in this case. And the Trial Chamber dealt with it where relevant. So our submission that the critical question is not whether the judgement recites verbatim all of the relevant jurisprudence; instead what is necessary to ask is whether the Trial Chamber actually applied those principles and exercised the appropriate caution in evaluating the evidence. When you look through the judgement you will see that the Trial Chamber did exactly that. For each incident, it carefully recorded the evidence on identification and then set out its analysis of that evidence. In its assessment of the identification evidence, the Trial Chamber addressed the pertinent factors. It took into account factors such as the conditions in which the witnesses saw Milan Lukic, including the time they spent in his presence; the traumatic or crowded circumstances; and the lighting in the relevant location. For example - and Mr. Visnjic deals with this question in relation to lighting - the lighting at Pionirska Street was litigated at length at trial. The Chamber took all of this evidence into account and explained at paragraph 597: "While some witnesses testified that the late hour and rain made observations difficult, witnesses consistently testified that light from sources including neighbouring houses and flash-lights carried by the men and their close proximity to the men, allowed them to identify the men who carried out the transfer." The Chamber also addressed factors such as witnesses' descriptions of Milan Lukic and the time elapsed since they had last seen him. Milan Lukic is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please slow down because it is difficult for us to follow and to follow your line of reasoning. So we need you to slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters. Milan Lukic's suggestion that the Chamber was reckless in its approach to identification evidence is undermined by the detailed treatment of this issue in the judgement. His attempts to relitigate these details on appeal should be dismissed. Milan Lukic suggests that a full procedure of identification parade or photo spread are mandatory and that no conviction is possible without having followed these procedures. In answer to that submission I refer Your Honours to the Kalimanzira appeal judgement at page 96: "Neither the rules nor the jurisprudence of the Tribunal oblige a Trial Chamber to require a particular type of identification evidence." The Trial Chamber also carefully differentiated between witnesses who knew or were familiar with Milan Lukic and those who were not. In the process, the Trial Chamber took note of the well-accepted common sense proposition that recognition evidence, that is, evidence from witnesses who had prior knowledge of or familiarity with the accused, is generally more reliable than evidence from the witnesses who see the accused for the first time at crime scenes. The Trial Chamber carefully assessed the recognition witness accounts, including the basis for their prior knowledge of or familiarity with Milan Lukic. And this approach that the Trial Chamber took is supported by the Tribunal jurisprudence that is cited in our Prosecution response brief at paragraph 3. A more recent example than those cases cited of a Trial Chamber using knowledge of an accused as a relevant factor to identification is in the Popovic trial judgement at paragraph 55. In that judgement the Trial Chamber noted: "In assessing identification evidence, the Trial Chamber has taken into account a number of relevant factors, including: The circumstances in which each witness claimed to have observed the accused; the length of the observation; the familiarity of the witness with the accused prior to the identification; and the description given by the witness of his or her identification of the accused." I also refer you to a similar approach taken earlier by the Kordic and Cerkez Trial Chamber at paragraph 725 of its judgement which was approved by the Appeals Chamber judgement at paragraph 704. So in our submission, the Chamber's detailed treatment of this evidence is consistent with its cautious approach to identification evidence in general. Let me turn to the issue of in-court recognitions. As was pointed out earlier, during trial several witnesses made in-court recognitions of Milan Lukic as the person whom they saw at various crime scenes. As the Chamber pointed out, the in-court recognitions were not relied on with one exception, and it's our position that as a result the in-court recognitions were largely irrelevant, particularly given the fact that the assessment of their use was made by a professional Trial Chamber that would not have been influenced in any way by the in-court recognition if it did not rely on it. In any event, Milan Lukic fails to show that the in-court identifications by witnesses that were familiar with the accused at the time of the crime are impermissible. It's our position that although the Limaj appeals judgement at paragraph 27 sets out a general rule that no weight should be placed on in-court identifications, there is in fact an exception for recognition witnesses. I refer you to the Simic Trial Chamber at paragraph 26: "The Trial Chamber also scrutinised the in-court identification of the accused by witnesses, noting that evidence on identification is generally viewed with caution, but also acknowledging, given the close-knit community from which both the accused and witnesses come, that identification evidence may carry more weight when considering its reliability where witnesses have prior knowledge of the accused." Moreover, the domestic criminal courts that Milan Lukic cites in support of his proposition that in-court recognitions are impermissible are not on point as they do not involve in-court identifications by recognition witnesses. Like international criminal tribunals, domestic cases involving in-court identifications by recognition witnesses find no error in the procedure. For the cases on this point, I refer Your Honours to footnote 21 of the Prosecution response brief. Your Honours, in conclusion on the point of identification, the Chamber took a careful and thorough approach to the issue. The judgement shows that it addressed this evidence in detail in relation to each of the crime sites. Milan Lukic ignores the extensive analysis in the judgement and seeks to relitigate the issue on appeal. However, I would submit that he fails to show that the Chamber erred in its approach to identification and his challenges should be dismissed. Let me now move to the two killings at Pionirska Street and Bikavac that I am dealing with. I will first provide Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to slow down for the purposes of the interpretation. It is really too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: -- with a brief review of the core facts of Pionirska Street and Bikavac to give my submissions context. First, on June 14th, 1992, a small group of armed men dressed in camouflage uniforms, including Milan and Sredoje Lukic, first robbed then terrorised over 60 Muslims from Koritnik, mainly from the Kurspahic clan, at the Memic house on Pionirska Street in Visegrad. Later the same day, Milan Lukic and his armed group herded them into the nearby Omeragic house. Milan Lukic set fire to the house. The Muslims who escaped or attempted were shot at. Several Muslims died attempting to escape. At least 58 Muslims were either burned alive or shot to death. Two weeks later, Milan Lukic and a small group of armed men dressed in camouflage uniforms again herded a large group of Muslims into a house across town in Bikavac. Again Milan Lukic set the house on fire, burning the victims to death, and shot at those who attempted to escape. Approximately 60 Muslims perished. After hearing the testimony from Muslim survivors of Pionirska Street and Bikavac, including those who knew Milan Lukic personally and observed him as he lit the fires, the Trial Chamber reasonably found that he was criminally responsible for both of these brutal massacres. The Trial Chamber appropriately summed up the killings when it stated at paragraph 740: "In an all too long, sad and wretched history of man's inhumanity to man, the Pionirska Street and Bikavac fires must rank high ... these horrific events remain imprinted on the memory for the viciousness of the incendiary attack, for the obvious premeditation and calculation that defined it, for the sheer callousness, monstrosity, and brutality of herding, trapping, and locking the victims into the two houses, thereby rendering them helpless in the ensuing inferno and for the degree of pain and suffering inflicted on the victims as they were burnt alive." Starting with Pionirska Street. Milan Lukic challenges the factual basis of his convictions for Pionirska Street but fails to show that the Trial Chamber erred. Survivors of the Pionirska Street killing consistently stated that Milan Lukic carried out the crimes. These first-hand witnesses who came from the same small community as Milan Lukic include some who personally knew him and recognised him as he perpetrated the crimes. Seven survivors identified Milan Lukic as one of the perpetrators of the crimes committed at Pionirska Street. All of these witnesses were found to be credible and reliable by the Trial Chamber. The survivors of Milan Lukic's crimes described the events of June 14th in detail. Between 4.00 and 5.00 p.m. Milan Lukic arrived at the Memic house on Pionirska Street. He was armed and wearing a camouflage uniform. He was with other armed men in camouflage uniform including people identified as Sredoje Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and Milan Susnjar, or Lalco, together I'll call them the Lukic group. Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic entered the Memic house and introduced themselves to the group of over 60 unarmed Muslims inside. The group was mainly composed of women and girls, the elderly and children, including babies. A large percentage of the people inside knew Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic and Susnjar, and were able to identify them on sight. Two of the witnesses that recognised Milan Lukic when he entered the Memic house are sisters VG-101 and VG-78. Both sisters knew Milan Lukic and went to school with him for a number of years. They described how he played a leading role in the series of crimes committed by the armed Serb perpetrators throughout the day and night at Pionirska Street. Milan Lukic does not dispute that VG-101 went to school with him, saw him on a daily basis, and after finishing school continued to see him at dances and parties. He does not dispute that VG-78 went to school with him for several years and saw him at school. His complaint is that the circumstances of their identification do not -- were not sufficient for them to be able to identify him beyond a reasonable doubt. In Mitar Vasiljevic the Trial Chamber concluded that they had a reasonable doubt as to whether Mitar Vasiljevic was among the armed group at Pionirska Street. The Defence suggests that the reasonable doubt of -- in Mitar Vasiljevic should be transposed to this case and that there should be an automatic acquittal because the evidence of VG-101 and VG-78 among the other evidence was not sufficient to satisfy it that the evidence proved Mitar Vasiljevic's presence beyond a reasonable doubt. But he ignores the fact that Trial Chambers in other cases can take different positions based on the evidence that they hear. The evidence of VG-101 and VG-78 was before this Trial Chamber. The testimony, live testimony, that VG-101 and VG-78 gave was tested and they were examined fully on inconsistencies between their testimony before the Lukic Trial Chamber and the Vasiljevic Trial Chamber. This Trial Chamber performed a full review and analysis and came to a reasoned decision on what part of their testimony to accept. And I would submit that the Trial Chamber was entitled based on the evidence that it heard, based on their analysis and consideration of the demeanour and presentation of the evidence by the witnesses, both in examination-in-chief and cross-examination, to find that VG-101 and VG-78 recognised him at Pionirska Street. These witnesses, VG-78, 101, and others, provided consistent and mutually corroborating accounts of Milan Lukic's actions. After Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic introduced themselves, Milan Lukic ordered the Muslims to surrender their valuables and threatened to put a bullet in the head of anyone who withheld anything. Milan Lukic robbed the Muslim civilians at gunpoint. The women and children were segregated from the group and strip-searched. Milan Lukic later removed at least three women from the house. They were subsequently raped. Subsequently Milan Lukic and his armed group left the Memic house, but before leaving, Milan Lukic told the Muslim civilians that no one was allowed to leave until he returned. Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, and other members of the group returned later that evening. All were still armed and in camouflage. They transferred the Koritnik group to the Omeragic house, a distance of about 20 to 30 metres. The Omeragic house had been prepared with fire accelerant. The Lukic group was organised as observed by VG-84 who stated: "There was a light in front of the house, they had flash-lights. Everything had been prepared in advance." And his evidence is consistent with evidence provided by several other witnesses, including VG-38. The Muslim civilians were told that they were being transferred for their safety and that they did not need their shoes or luggage. As Milan Lukic was transferring the victims from the Omeragic house, VG-13 passed him within 30 centimetres. Once the victims were locked in the Omeragic house, they realised that they were not safe there. VG-13 and other witnesses described how the air in the room was suffocating due to the presence of a pungent, sticky substance on the carpets which caused persons to choke. After the Muslim civilians had been trapped in the Omeragic house for a short time, Milan Lukic placed an explosive device inside which detonated and set the room on fire, enveloping the people inside it. Milan Lukic and other of his armed group positioned outside the house shot at members of the Koritnik group who tried to escape. In total they killed at least 58 Muslim civilians at the Omeragic house. VG-13 knew Milan Lukic prior to the incident, saw him place the explosive device inside the Omeragic house, and saw him when he shot her as she escaped through the window. The Milan Lukic Defence has argued that VG-13 was not a recognition witness. However, the paragraph that it refers to in the OTP closing brief concerns in-court identification. The Trial Chamber did not rely on VG-13's in-court identification. Moreover, the Trial Chamber explained the basis for her prior knowledge of Milan Lukic in the judgement at paragraphs 408 and 599. I just read paragraph 408 of the judgement. "During examination-in-chief, VG-13 stated that the first time that she saw Milan Lukic was on June 14, 1992. However, under cross-examination she testified that she had seen Milan Lukic prior to the incident in the area in which she lived, and that the last time she saw him '[h]e was around 20, maybe a little bit over 20.' She sometimes saw Milan Lukic about twice a year 'in passing' when he would go to the Panos hotel. However, VG-13 stated, 'I have no ... personal knowledge about Milan Lukic. He was a neighbour who was growing up in our proximity, and I cannot say anything else.'" There's nothing unreasonable about the Trial Chamber's finding. The standard on appeal is whether there was an error in the judgement and I would submit that based on the Trial Chamber's treatment in paragraph 408 there was no error. Milan Lukic suggests that there was no light inside the house at all and so VG-13 could not have recognised him as the person who placed the explosive device inside the door. That's found in his argument today and his reply brief at paragraph 72. However, as I mentioned previously, the Chamber carefully addressed the issue of lighting. It noted that light came from various sources, including neighbouring houses and perpetrators' flash-lights, enabling the victims in the Omeragic house to see the perpetrators. Additionally, there was light into the room from the street lights outside, as was stated in judgement paragraph 366. VG-13 knew Milan Lukic and provided compelling evidence of seeing him set the Omeragic house on fire. She was cross-examined at length, suggesting that she did not know him and that she could not have seen him and that the fire never happened. The Trial Chamber sat through this evidence, through this cross-examination, and addressed Milan Lukic's challenges to her in the judgement. It found that VG-13 knew him prior to the Pionirska Street crimes, that she was a credible and reliable witness. On appeal he simply seeks to substitute the Chamber's interpretation of the evidence with his own. Along with VG-13 and the other witnesses who knew Milan Lukic prior to the crimes committed at Pionirska Street, several additional witnesses identified him as one of the perpetrators. VG-38, VG-18, VG-84, and Huso Kurspahic, who conveyed the account of his deceased father Hasib Kurspahic, all described how Milan Lukic was a member of the small group of perpetrators. The Trial Chamber heard their accounts, assessed their evidence, their demeanour, and concluded their evidence was credible and reliable. With respect to Milan Lukic's arguments about Mitar Vasiljevic's presence on Pionirska Street on 14 June 1992, these have already been fully addressed in the Prosecution response brief, other than to highlight one point. At paragraphs 81 and 82 of his reply, Sredoje Lukic states that the Prosecution misunderstands the jurisprudence governing adjudicated facts. It is Milan Lukic who misunderstands. While the Chamber initially admitted adjudicated facts from the Vasiljevic proceedings which would have supported the appellant's arguments, it subsequently heard live testimony to the contrary and rejected those adjudicated facts. And this is entirely consistent with the governing jurisprudence as set out in the Prosecution's response at paragraph 134. And again, just to point out that the Defence for Milan Lukic assumes that reasonable doubt by the Vasiljevic Trial Chamber conclusively decides that Mitar Vasiljevic was not there. And our position is clearly this is wrong logic. It is -- in any event this was the reason that Judge Robinson still found Milan Lukic guilty for the Pionirska crimes even though he dissented as to Vasiljevic's presence. I refer you to paragraphs 1.110 to 1.111. The issue of Vasiljevic's presence does not affect the Chamber's unanimous conclusion that several witnesses reliably place Milan Lukic at Pionirska Street on 14 June 1992. Let me turn to Bikavac. Our position is that Milan Lukic was properly convicted for the crimes at the Meho Aljic house in Bikavac and that he fails to demonstrate any error in the Chamber's findings. Approximately two weeks after the attack on Pionirska Street, Milan Lukic did it again. This time at least 60 Muslim civilians were killed. Just one person survived. On or about the evening of 27 June, Milan Lukic drove to the neighbourhood of Bikavac with music blaring from two cars, one a Passat, he and his armed companions went into the nearby houses and herded the occupants onto the street. These people included both residents and refugees. The people were told to file inside the house of Meho Aljic. Such was their fear, they complied without question. Once inside, the people were crowded into a single room whose exits were blocked and barricaded. Once Milan Lukic had herded everyone inside he blocked the last exit to the house. Milan Lukic and his companions threw sticks at the house, shot at it, and threw grenades inside. Shortly after, Milan Lukic set the house on fire. Just one person survived. The sole survivor was Zehra Turjacanin. Like other witnesses and victims in this case, she had known Milan Lukic. She had known him from childhood when she was at school. Milan Lukic was in the same class as her brother. She saw him as an adult too, recalling at least two occasions earlier in June 1992 when she saw him in Visegrad at the Alhos factory and at her neighbour's house, where she was drinking coffee. The Trial Chamber had no doubt about her prior knowledge of Milan Lukic. The Trial Chamber heard over three trial days Zehra Turjacanin's testimony. The Trial Judges sat with her as she described her attack and her inability to save her family from the flames. They saw her distress, they saw her disability caused by her burns.
