On the basis of a very careful and very personal scrutiny, the Trial Chamber was unequivocal in its assessment of Zehra Turjacanin's evidence, which it considered in its entirety. It found it to be coherent and reliable. The Trial Chamber was convinced that she was a witness of truth. The Trial Judges deserve great deference in their finding. So when Milan Lukic came to Zehra Turjacanin's house on the evening on or about 27 June, she recognised him instantly. She knew exactly who it was who told her and her family to assemble in the street and ordered them into Meho Aljic's house. She knew exactly who it was who pulled the gold necklace off her neck as she filed inside. And as she escaped the burning house, forced to abandon some of her closest family members, she knew exactly who she was escaping from. Moreover, Milan Lukic knew that the intended -- his intended victim had recognised him. As -- and we know this because he bothered to put a price on Zehra Turjacanin's head once he learned that she had escaped. Zehra Turjacanin's compelling evidence of Milan Lukic's attack was directly corroborated by Witness 58 and Witness 115, both of whom were previously acquainted with Milan Lukic. VG-58 was a neighbour and VG-115 had regular passing encounters. These witnesses were hiding nearby the Aljic house and observed the attack. They confirmed that Milan Lukic herded the people inside, that he shot at the house, and that he threw grenades and petrol. VG-58 heard him exhorting his companions to get as many people in as possible. VG-58 saw Zehra Turjacanin escape. Zehra Turjacanin's account was also confirmed by the story she told immediately after her escape, when her first action was to warn her neighbours. Having gone first to the house of Ismeta Kasapovic, who was not a witness, she went to the house of VG-35 and CW-2 and told them what had happened. She urged them to flee and to warn others. Earlier that day Milan Lukic had raped VG-35, having introduced himself the night before. Zehra Turjacanin then went to the house where VG-119 and VG-94 were staying. She told them the same story. Finally, Zehra Turjacanin's story was further confirmed by the evidence of Milan Lukic's condition after the attack. Before he went to Bikavac at about 8.00 p.m., Milan Lukic had visited VG-94 and VG-119, driving in the red Passat. They told the two women that they would be killed if they left their home. The Trial Chamber determined that they would be able -- that they were able to recognise Milan Lukic from their encounters. About two hours later, Milan Lukic returned, and I refer you to paragraph 721 for that point I just made. Again, he returned in a red Passat. He was dripping with sweat, dirty, and looked and smelled like he had been near a fire. The Trial Chamber emphasised that the testimony of VG-94 and VG-119 strongly reinforces that of Zehra Turjacanin and it gave great weight to their testimony. Let me now move to the question, question 1, asked by the Appeals Chamber. And the answer that I will give applies equally to the Pionirska Street and Bikavac massacres. The Trial Chamber properly analysed the killings at Pionirska Street and Bikavac separately and found that each independently were sufficiently large to constitute extermination in the circumstances of this case. First, the number of victims at each killing site is consistent with previous incidents that have been judicially classified as extermination. The numbers here are 58 at Pionirska Street and 60 at Bikavac. Although there is no specific numerical threshold for extermination, the jurisprudence of the international tribunals indicates that the killing of over 50 victims is sufficiently large scale to qualify as extermination. In Brdjanin, the Appeals Chamber held that the killing of 68 persons at Brisevo was an independent act of extermination. The Milan Lukic Defence argues that in Brdjanin the Appeals Chamber only found that the total number of 1.669 deaths qualified as extermination; that is incorrect. At paragraph 472 of the Brdjanin appeal judgement, the Appeals Chamber clearly found that each of the separate killing sites, including Brisevo, was sufficiently large to qualify as extermination. He also argues that the Vasiljevic Trial Chamber required that there be a vast scheme of collective murder. This is incorrect. The Stakic appeal judgement at paragraph 258 stated that the jurisprudence of the Tribunal does not support requirements of either a vast scheme of collective murder or knowledge of such a scheme. Additionally he misreads the Martic trial judgement at paragraphs 404 and 405. The Trial Chamber held that various killings could not be accumulated. The Trial Chamber did not comment that 165 victims was an insufficiently large number. There are trial judgements of other international tribunals which have found that the killing of over 50 people is sufficiently large scale. One connect -- appeals judgement that I refer you to is the Sesay appeal judgement which confirms findings of extermination for 63 victims, 30 and 40 victims, and 64 victims, respectively, confirming the Trial Chamber's finding in that case. Mr. Gillett will deal with that more specifically tomorrow in the Prosecution appeal. Milan Lukic seeks to raise the threshold for extermination to require killings of thousands of victims over extensive periods of time at various locations. But he omits to mention that the killing of an extremely large number of victims far exceeding the threshold required for extermination can be an aggravating factor in sentencing. So our submission is on a numerical basis, the massacres at Pionirska Street and Bikavac each qualify as extermination. Secondly, the circumstances. In addition to the number of victims, the Chamber noted the contextual factors surrounding the killings and to further confirm that they each qualified as extermination. As the Chamber correctly noted, the Pionirska Street was a single mass killing, not a series of unrelated individual murders. The victims were targeted and were mainly residents from a small village, Koritnik, and were mostly from the same extended family, the Kurspahics. The method used shows the intent to kill all the victims. Similarly in Bikavac, the method was similar. Even without these contextual factors, the Chamber's findings remain valid on the numbers of victims killed in each incident. The murder was large scale and Milan Lukic has not shown that the Chamber erred in respect of its findings that he committed extermination at both locations. Our position and submission is that on the basis of the trial evidence, including the testimony from survivors who personally knew Milan Lukic and observed him as he lit the fires, the Trial Chamber reasonably found him responsible for both of the brutal and callous massacres. Milan Lukic has failed to demonstrate any reversible errors in the trial judgement and his appeals on the third and fourth grounds of appeal should be dismissed. Subject to any questions you may have, I will pass the podium to Ms. Monchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHUSTER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Between June 1992 and the beginning of 1993, Milan Lukic came to the Uzamnica detention camp many, many times. He savagely assaulted, again and again, many of the Muslim detainees who were held there under deplorable living conditions. Milan Lukic was not a guard at the camp. He would simply stop by to mistreat the Muslims as he pleased. He kicked them, he beat them with his fists, with stakes, with a pole, and with wooden bats. He shocked them with an electric baton. Once, when the bat he was using broke because he was beating a man so hard, he would simply get a new bat and continue the beating. Milan Lukic's basic claim is that he was never at the camp. This should be rejected by Your Honours. The Trial Chamber carefully and in much detail assessed the evidence of the four witnesses, who all saw Lukic at the camp on many occasions and who all corroborate each other. All of these witnesses were adamant about one thing: The man who kicked and beat them so savagely many, many times was no other than Milan Lukic. Some of the witnesses said that Milan came so often they even learned to recognise his voice, and I refer Your Honours specifically to Witnesses Berberovic, that's transcript 1953, and Dervisevic, that's transcript 1953 -- sorry, Berberovic is 2510. The witnesses did not give generic descriptions of Milan Lukic, as was posited this morning. I refer to our brief in this regard for the details. That Witness Dervisevic's eyesight barred him from identifying anyone is mere speculation. The Defence already raised this at trial and the Trial Chamber considered this evidence, 804 of the trial judgement. But more importantly, three of the witnesses learned Milan Lukic's identity at the camp. They were told by a man named Saban Muratagic or by other inmates. Muratagic was some sort of a watchman at the camp. He knew Milan because they came from neighbouring villages and they had gone to school together. That's what he told them -- that's what he told Witness Berberovic and Witness Dervisevic. The witnesses all also provided other biographical data that they learned at the time, that they learned about the man who regularly came to the camp to beat them and who they saw many, many times. They correctly stated that Milan Lukic came from Rujiste, that he had worked in Serbia prior to the war, that he came with his cousin Sredoje Lukic, that he was under 30 years old, and other details. Like one witness mentioned that Milan Lukic had been imprisoned for a train kidnapping, a fact which Milan Lukic himself confirmed in court when he gave his final statement. There is nothing that would indicate that the witnesses only learned this information years after the events, as suggested by the Defence this morning. And I'll give you a short quotation from Witness Dervisevic's transcript testimony before the Trial Chamber, that's transcript 1962, and Dervisevic asked about how he learned about Milan Lukic's identity answered: "It was another man in detention, Saban Muratagic, who told me. I think Milan Lukic is from a village close to his village, Zupa. Milan is from Rujiste. He can confirm that. So this man knew him ..." Under these circumstances alone, the Chamber was entitled to find that it was Milan Lukic who beat the men. Your Honours, in this regard I refer you to paragraph 196 of the Rukundo appeals judgement where the Appeals Chamber held that a Chamber can rely on the evidence of witnesses who learned of the identity of their abuser through other persons. The fact that Saban Muratagic, from who Berberovic and Dervisevic heard it was Milan Lukic who beat them, was not cross-examined by the Defence does not matter in this regard. In any case, the Defence had ample opportunity to call Mr. Muratagic himself. In fact, he appeared on their 65 ter list. Now, the Chamber also had the evidence of VG-25, a Rule 92 quater witness who did know Milan Lukic before the war and who also said that he was regularly beaten by Lukic at the camp. Because VG-25 did not testify in person, the Chamber was very careful when taking his evidence into account. But it found that VG-25 simply corroborated the testimony of the three viva voce witnesses. In turn, their testimony corroborated his. The Chamber also considered that these four men were all held together for about eight months in the same hangar. It found that VG-25 would have confirmed the other detainees' knowledge of Milan Lukic. Your Honours, Milan Lukic also complains about the fact that the Chamber relied on Berberovic's and Dervisevic's in-court confirmation of him. But contrary to what we heard this morning, the Chamber did not put much emphasis on this. Given that both of these witnesses saw Lukic many, many times at the camp, even recognising his voice, it simply accepted their pointing out to Lukic in the courtroom as part of the larger process of establishing his identity. And again, the Chamber did not need to rely on the in-court confirmation because it already had much evidence that the witnesses recognised Milan Lukic at the camp. Second, Your Honour, as a practical matter, in circumstances like there were prevailing at Uzamnica camp, the Chamber should be able to rely on such evidence, otherwise victims of crimes that went on for long periods of time, such as unlawful detention or enslavement, would be excluded as recognition witnesses even though they had lots of opportunity, as in this case, to become acquainted with their abuser. Your Honours, four witnesses told the Chamber the same account; that is, while they were detained under terrible circumstances, Milan Lukic added to their misery by savagely beating and kicking them on many occasions as he pleased and simply because he could. The Chamber accepted their consistent and comprehensive evidence and correctly convicted Milan Lukic for cruel treatment and inhumane acts in relation to Uzamnica camp. This concludes my submissions. Unless you have further questions, I would pass on to my colleague Virginie Monchy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MONCHY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Trial Chamber convicted Milan Lukic for the murders at the Drina River, the Varda factory, and for the murder of Hajra Koric on the basis of solid eye-witness evidence and all of these witnesses knew Milan Lukic before the murders. All challenges raised by Milan Lukic this morning have been addressed in detail in our written submissions. Turning -- I will briefly be turning to the Drina River, the Varda killings, and, if I have any time left, to the Koric murder. The eye-witnesses' evidence of -- concerning the Drina River incident. The eye-witness evidence of the two survivors VG-32 and VG-14 and the evidence of Milan Lukic's accomplice, Mitar Vasiljevic, is credible and reliable. The Trial Chamber reasonably relied on VG-14's and VG-32's prior knowledge of Milan Lukic; second, on their immediate recognition of him on the 7th of June and on their similar description to him. Contrary to what the Defence has been asserting this morning, the Trial Chamber did not rely on the in-court confirmation that Milan Lukic was the man who shot them. VG-14 and VG-32 are recognition witnesses because VG-14 knew Milan Lukic from secondary school which they attended together at the age of 16 and 17. And he recognised him immediately when Milan Lukic entered his house to take him away. Concerning the issue of a mole that has been addressed this morning, it has been explored at length at the trial and in the trial judgement. And I will refer Your Honours to judgement paragraph 129 to 131, and 201. VG-32 knew Milan Lukic because he had seem him twice at least before the murders and he had been told who Milan Lukic was. He recognised him as soon as Lukic approached the house of his father-in-law to kidnap him. And in addition, when VG-32 was detained in the house after Milan Lukic had kidnapped him, he heard one of the men guarding them referring to Milan Lukic by his name. In concluding that both witnesses recognised Milan Lukic on the 7th of June, the Trial Chamber reasonably considered that both witnesses gave very similar descriptions of Milan Lukic and that they were exposed to Milan Lukic, often at close range, for several hours and during daylight. And I just have a small specification to make with respect to one of the Defence allegations in his reply brief. VG-32 described Milan Lukic's physical appearance and this is in Exhibit 1D30 at page 242. Turning now to Mitar Vasiljevic. The Trial Chamber considered the Defence's argument that Vasiljevic had an incentive to lie about Milan Lukic's involvement. But it reasonably rejected it on the basis that Vasiljevic's evidence corroborated VG-14's and actually VG-32's evidence. And this is at judgement paragraph 195. And the Defence doesn't show that -- that this was unreasonable. As to the Defence allegation this morning that Vasiljevic, knowing that Milan Lukic will not be arrested, implicated him, this is purely speculative and contrary to the evidence. And I will refer Your Honours to the Prosecution final trial brief at paragraph 45 and 46. Turning now to the Varda factory murders. There was solid evidence that Milan Lukic was the shooter. The Trial Chamber reasonably relied on the evidence of the two main eye-witnesses, VG-24 and VG-42, to convict Milan Lukic for the Varda factory murders. It reasonably found that they first knew him from before; and second, that they both recognised Milan Lukic as the killer and that their evidence was corroborative of one another as to his actions. Concerning VG-24 and VG-42's prior knowledge of Milan Lukic, this issue has been -- sorry, Your Honour. This issue has been carefully analysed by the Trial Chamber and the Trial Chamber reasonably considered VG-24's testimony that he knew Milan Lukic when he was 12 or 13 years old and that she knew his family. It also properly considered that VG-24 knew Milan Lukic well because in 1992, before the murders, he had become a regular visitor to the Varda factory where VG-24 worked. As for VG-42, the Trial Chamber reasonably found that she knew Milan Lukic before the murders. She knew him as a child, as mentioned by the Defence this morning, because his -- her son, sorry, had been friends with Milan Lukic; but also because her father was a close friend of Milan Lukic's grandfather and because of so -- she knew Milan Lukic's parents and details of his life. The Trial Chamber -- the Judges considered that VG-42 had sometimes difficulties to understand the questions she was being asked or to remember dates. They also considered the inconsistencies in her evidence. However, having observed VG-42's demeanour during her testimony, they reasonably found that this did not undermine her clear and repeated evidence that she knew Milan Lukic well. Turning to my second point, both VG-24 and VG-42 recognised Milan Lukic and gave corroborative evidence as to his actions. Both witnesses saw the events and Milan Lukic from a different vantage point and over an extended period of time. VG-24 was inside the factory and saw Milan Lukic from very close. Witness VG-42 saw the same events from the balcony of the top floor of a house, a higher and unobstructed point of view. Both witnesses saw the workers -- Milan Lukic herd the workers towards the Drina River and lining them up in front of the water. VG-42 saw Milan Lukic killing the workers one after the other, while VG-24 heard a burst of fire. The Trial Chamber carefully considered the discrepancies between their evidence and it reasonably found that they resulted from the differences in their respective vantage points. The Trial Chamber was also well aware of a risk of misidentification with respect to VG-42 and it considered in detail the evidence challenges regarding her ability to recognise Milan Lukic from a location and it reasonably rejected them. And I will refer Your Honours to judgement paragraph 300, 321, 262, and 258. I have been indicated that I'm running out of time, so unless you have any questions I will conclude my submissions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I apologise in advance if we seem confused a bit, but I will provide one part of the response and the other part will be provided by Mr. Ivetic and we will be taking turns. I should like first to state that I agree fully with Mr. Kremer, that the key issue in this case is the issue of identity. As Judge Robinson said himself on transcript page 372 in this case. Judging by the number of the page, it must have been at the beginning of the trial. As the trial proceeded, I believe this assertion lost in weight, and finally, the reference made by Mr. Kremer to the principle applied by the Trial Chamber in deciding on the issue of identification to be found in paragraph 30 of the trial judgement indicates that there is nothing about the most important thing in this case. The quotation made by Mr. Kremer is from a footnote to that paragraph which as a secondary reference indicates the judgement in Haradinaj et al., which makes a passing reference to the Rules set out in the appeals judgement in Kupreskic. We believe this is an inadequate corroboration of the claims made by Mr. Kremer as to which standards were applied in the judgement. I believe the Appeals Chamber should have a real concern that adequate standards have not been consistently applied. Concerning identification evidence, the Prosecution asserts that regardless of everything, the Trial Chamber did apply relevant factors in relation to each crime site. In our appeal brief we claimed the opposite and we made our points very clearly. However, on one issue we can agree with Mr. Kremer, he emphasised that the witnesses are still traumatised by their experiences. However, nowhere in the judgement was consideration given to the effect of trauma on identifications made by the witnesses. Regarding the issue of identification in court, several legal sources have been quoted, including the judgement in Limaj, the appeal judgement in Limaj. In this connection I should like to say that in the Limaj case certain witnesses claimed they were able to identify and recognise the accused and identified him in the courtroom. And as we can see in paragraph 25 of this appeals judgement, the Chamber believed this procedure to be inappropriate. At issue was the accused, a camp guard known at the time under the name of Shala, and there were three witnesses. One of those was N-04 who described his assailant and said he learned his name after the war. Another witness, L-07, claimed that after the war the accused introduced himself as Shala. The third witness, L-10, said he heard that name from other detainees in the camp and that's how he was able to recognise the accused. The facts described are very similar to those in our case. However, it needs to be emphasised that the Prosecution in the Limaj case agreed that in-court identifications should not be given great weight without prior notice in the attempts to confirm the identity of the accused by the witnesses who recognise him. In any case, the Appeals Chamber in Limaj decided that no probative value should be attached to in-court identifications. Nevertheless, the Trial Chamber in this case cited the Limaj case in support of a totally opposite conclusion. Another case containing similar elements is Kamuhanda, where the probative value of identifications by three witnesses was considered. One witness, GAF, stated that before the incident he had seen the accused a number of times, and therefore the Appeals Chamber accepted that GAF had recognised the witness. By the standards applied in this case, Witness GAF would be a recognition witness. Another witness, GES, said in his statement that he had known the accused for three years. So the Appeals Chamber allowed the possibility that GES was able to recognise the accused. Again, by the standards in this case, Witness GES would be a recognition witness. A third witness, GAA, had seen the accused twice before when the accused had been pointed out to him. By the standards applied by the Prosecution in this case, Witness GAA would also be a recognition witness. However, the most important thing is and the most curious thing is that the Appeals Chamber in Kamuhanda case decided not to attach any weight to in-court identifications by these witnesses. The next point made by Mr. Kremer refers to a number of cases from our domestic system that both the Defence of Milan Lukic and the OTP refer to in their briefs. In our preparations for this hearing, we just found a case recently completed that would soon be argued before the Supreme Court of the United States and I would like the floor -- to give the floor briefly to Mr. Ivetic. He would need only two or three minutes to tell you something about this case called Henderson.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Kremer at page 25 of today's transcript said that neither the Rules nor the jurisprudence of the Tribunal oblige a Trial Chamber to require a particular type of identification evidence. But we would submit that ICTY Chambers should be mindful of developments as to identification evidence in the world around them in the various legal jurisdictions, so as to stay current with major legal trends. The issue of identification evidence is at the centre stage in the United States, where a case, New Jersey versus Henderson, which was just decided August 24th, 2011, by the Supreme Court of New Jersey, is scheduled to be heard by the United States Supreme Court in its November session. And it deals with recognising the serious concerns as to the existing modus of identification evidence in courts of law. And that's State versus Larry Henderson, number 62,218, and as I said, the New Jersey Supreme Court decided the case August 24th, 2011, and I'd like to quote just a few short selections from it. In the opinion of the -- in the opinion of the Supreme Court of New Jersey, the scientific evidence it reviewed -- the significant scientific evidence it reviewed showed: "Convincing proof that the current test for evaluating the trust-worthiness of eye-witness identifications should be revised" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel kindly slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will try. "Study after study revealed a troubling lack of reliability in eye-witness identifications. "We are convinced from the scientific evidence in the record that memory is malleable, and that an array of variables can affect and dilute memory and lead to misidentifications. Those factors include system variables like line-up procedures, which are within the control of the criminal justice system, and estimator variables like lighting conditions or the presence of a weapon, over which the legal system has no control." Your Honours, in promoting a change in the way the American courts view identification evidence, the New Jersey Supreme Court in its decision said: "At stake is the very integrity of the criminal justice system and the court's ability to conduct fair trials." Your Honours, we're only asking for the Appeals Chamber to ask its Chambers here to exercise the same diligence in examining the identification evidence and to recognise that although there is not a consensus as to the identification evidence, the -- the jurisprudence that Mr. Visnjic has set forth has identified factors that need to be taken into account and the very serious concerns with the manner in which the identification evidence in this case was handled. And I will return to him -- do you have any more? I will return to him for any more submissions on reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I should now like to turn to the assertions made by Mr. Kremer regarding VG-13. Mr. Kremer said that the problem with VG-13 was that in-court identification they made. What we said and what the Prosecution also stated in their appeal brief is that the Prosecution itself did not rely on VG-13 because he is not a recognition witness. That is the gist of the Prosecution's claim, and we believe that Mr. Kremer failed to explain this. As for other witnesses who had seen Milan Lukic, we have already stated in our earlier submissions today that especially with regard to VG-38 and VG-78 and VG-101, the Chamber should take into account also their identification of Mitar Vasiljevic on site, and then if the Chamber accepts Vasiljevic's alibi, then it should weigh the importance and the import of these statements with reference to Milan Lukic which the Trial Chamber failed to do. Regarding the Bikavac incident, I think we have dealt with it sufficiently in our appeal brief and earlier submissions. As regards the submissions on Uzamnica, the Prosecution says that as a practical matter we should rely on identification evidence when a person's identity becomes known during a beating in this case. From the viewpoint of the Prosecution that is possible; however, as a matter of principle, protection must be ensured to the accused under those circumstances. The key issue here that pertains to the practical matter raised by the OTP was why they didn't take recourse to out-of-court identification or similar procedures in the preliminary investigation processes. We submit that it shouldn't be permissible for the accused to be identified for the first time in the court, as it was the case under present circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Ivetic would like to add something with relation to extermination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will be brief again, Your Honours. Returning to extermination. First Judge Liu's second question to the Prosecution. Bikavac is not a separate village. Bikavac is simply a neighbourhood within Visegrad town. In both instances, the killings are not said to have taken place in the respective villages, but are said to have taken place in Visegrad town itself, with a population of 20.000 persons. If we were to consider the contextual factors, such as the population, an accused must also be shown to have known about these contextual factors. I think I'm right in saying that there was no evidence that Milan Lukic knew what the size of the group from Koritnik was in relation to the population of that village. So I think that this is not the right case to start introducing that as a specific legal test for extermination. I stress as to Bikavac the victims were from several different villages and the Trial Chamber focused not on their origin but on their status as being vulnerable in its analysis. That's at trial judgement paragraph 949. So again, there is inconsistency and error in the Chamber's -- the Trial Chamber's approach. Now turning to the Prosecution's submissions of today, which we say misstate the holdings of relevant jurisprudence which they cite. Paragraph 472 of Brdjanin does not separately say that Brisevo was extermination. The paragraph cumulates each site. The number of those killed in Brisevo was considered in light of the surrounding circumstances, i.e., the other killings occurring at that time. And that would be paragraph 472 of Brdjanin. And, in fact, if we look at the actual text of that holding, Your Honours, since the parties -- this is the Chamber -- the Appeals Chamber: "Since the parties do not challenge the Trial Chamber's decision to consider all of the killings in the territory of the ARK as a whole rather than to distinguish them by location and incident, the Appeals Chamber need not consider this issue. Suffice it to say that with respect to these specific incidents cited by the Prosecution which involved the killing of between 68 and 300 people in each of the five locations, the Appeals Chamber is satisfied that the actus reus of the crime of extermination was made out." And I stress the final line of that holding, which is: "... the Appeals Chamber considers that the scale of the killings in light of the circumstances in which they occurred meets the required threshold of massiveness for the purposes of extermination." So again, the Prosecution is not right. With regard to Martic, the Prosecution again is not right, Your Honours. Paragraph 404 says: "Having considered these factors as well as the totality of the evidence surrounding the killing incidents charged as extermination, the Trial Chamber finds that the evidence is insufficient to establish that the crime of extermination was committed on an accumulated basis." I also direct you to look at paragraph 405, where the Trial Chamber said: "Even in the case of two killings in an organised and callous manner, the Trial Chamber said it can't" -- that: "These killings, even taken together, cannot be considered as having been committed on a large scale." Continuing the quotation of the Chamber: "In other words, the killings at Krecane near Bacin do not meet the element of massiveness required for extermination." So again we believe Martic supports our point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Try to conclude, please, because we are coming very close to the limit of the time available for the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me just finish one thing quickly. I add simply that massiveness in plain English suggests a large number. Again, we are not inviting the Appeals Chamber to set a minimum, but there must be a large number or else the distinction between murder and extermination becomes impossible to maintain. We submit there is no need to introduce such uncertainty at this late stage of the Tribunal's life. And I would turn the floor over to Mr. Visnjic for one quick point that he has. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just two brief submissions. One relates to in-court identification. The Prosecution did not reply to our submission regarding the prejudice -- prejudicial nature of the repeated in-court identification. And if it is believed by them that this procedure was completely useless, then they shouldn't have attempted it at all in the course of the proceedings. The second issue relates to general issues concerning the findings of the Trial Chamber in this case. The findings of the Trial Chamber in this case can be applied only if the Appeals Chamber is happy with the fact that the Trial Chamber has applied law in a proper way. This is not the case in Milan Lukic case at least as far as problems with identification are concerned. For that reason we believe that the Appeals Chamber in that respect should make a corrigendum to the trial judgement as contained in our final brief and in our oral submissions made today. Thank you on behalf of Mr. Ivetic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: If I could just have ten seconds to complete the answer to Judge Liu's question, paragraph 335 deals with the size of Koritnik, about 60 people, mixed Serbs and Muslims. My understanding of the evidence itself is it was primarily Muslims. The second point about Bratunac, it is a suburb or a small suburb or part of Visegrad -- or Bikavac, I'm sorry. Bikavac, a small neighbourhood in -- near Visegrad, and Mr. Ivetic is correct that the people there were -- that were subject to the attack were primarily residents and refugees from other villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We shall now make a break of one hour for lunch and our proceedings will be resumed at 14.45. The hearing is adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.26 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session and I would like to call upon the representatives of Sredoje Lukic. I have two questions to which the parties should answer before they present their submissions. First question regarding the events at the Uzamnica camp regarding the eighth ground of appeal for Sredoje Lukic. The Trial Chamber notes with concern that the photo-spread used with Adem Berberovic is missing. In the absence of the photo-spread, the Trial Chamber is not in a position to assess whether Adem Berberovic recognised Sredoje Lukic in the photo-spread or not. I invite the parties to talk about this issue, to develop this topic, taking into account the possibility that this evidence could be exculpatory and that Sredoje Lukic was not indicted specifically for having killed this victim. The second question is the following. The Trial Chamber conclude that in March 1993 and the first part of April 1993 -- Milan Lukic appealed this conclusion in his sixth ground of appeal. I would like to invite the parties to assess the potential impact on the appeal of Sredoje Lukic. In other words, to assess the impact of Milan Lukic's detention on the conviction of Sredoje Lukic. And now I would like to ask the counsels for Sredoje Lukic to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for the questions that you have put. As stated in our appeal ground number eight, we were astounded by such position taken by the Prosecution and to this date the material that we pointed out has not been disclosed to us. In other words, the chief of OTP investigation team, Ib Jul Hansen, clearly said in his evidence before this Tribunal and confirmed that no photo of my client, Sredoje Lukic, was used for the purposes of identification. Moreover, when we speak about the Pionirska Street incident, in addition to the appeals ground, I would like to highlight the following fact. The other two witnesses on which the Chamber wishes to base their conclusion relating to Uzamnica, that is to say, Witnesses Nurko Dervisevic and Islam Kustura, immediately after being released from detention gave statements to authorised police investigators. In those statements they named a large number of perpetrators and not a single one of the two gave the name of Sredoje Lukic. Moreover, Nurko Dervisevic actually gave three statements marked 2D15, 2D16, and 2D17, whereas Mr. Kustura's statement is 2D19. I would like to make reference to His Honour Judge May and his book entitled: "Evidence in International Criminal Law." [In English] Actually, "International Criminal Evidence," paragraph 7.89, pages 242 and 243, best available evidence. [Interpretation] If we are to apply this rule, then these statements in Uzamnica case and the lack of identification that we pointed out in our appeal would inevitably lead to exoneration of Mr. Sredoje Lukic as far as this incident is concerned. I will add one sentence only to this. Witness VG-25 mentioned by my learned friend Schuster from the OTP testified in favour of my client by saying that he had never come to Uzamnica camp. I believe that the appeal arguments and the submissions that I am making right now are quite sufficient for Mr. Sredoje Lukic to be relieved of any responsibility for this incident. Thank you. With your leave, I might add one more sentence. In paragraph 839 of the judgement, it is stated that the witness did not know Sredoje Lukic well, and when asked to describe him, to describe Sredoje Lukic, neither Islam Kustura or Adem Berberovic were capable of doing so in a proper way. Thank you for your attention once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid the mikes were not activated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We have got nothing to add in the interest of time, Your Honour, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have an hour and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would like now to say a few words about the Pionirska Street incident, but before I start my submission I would be grateful if, with your leave, I can distribute the tables that I gave to court officers which contain crucial parts from the judgement and our appeal brief and our submissions. This will facilitate the presentation that Professor Knoops and I are going to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the opinion of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Cepic before the break gave me a copy of the PowerPoint and the table. I have no objection to it being given to the members of the Panel. He also, just to forecast an issue, gave me a copy of the submissions by Mr. Knoops. I haven't had time to read them because I just read them which he's proposing to give to the Legal Officers after. I'll state my position once I've had an opportunity to review it. But for the PowerPoint and the table, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there aren't any objections, you can distribute those documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I will be kindly -- I would kindly ask the Legal Officers to provide the Honourable Judges with the copies of our presentation. [Interpretation] Your Honours, as you can see the table consists of three pages, the first one is robbery in Pionirska Street, the second page is the transfer, and the third one will accompany Professor Knoops' presentation and the standards advocated before this Tribunal. My presentation will be rather brief. I'll try and do it within the next 20 minutes and I will leave the rest of the time to Professor Knoops, whereas my learned friend Mr. Dieckmann will respond to the Prosecutor's appeal tomorrow. We claim that Mr. Lukic was not in Pionirska Street. It hasn't been proven beyond a reasonable doubt that Sredoje Lukic was present and that he participated in the incident. Professor Knoops and I will answer the three key issues with regard to this incident. The first question is this: Was Sredoje Lukic present at the Pionirska Street incident? Question number two: Even if the Chamber finds that Sredoje Lukic was indeed there, has it been proven beyond reasonable doubt that he was armed? And question number three: Even if the Chamber finds that Sredoje Lukic was there, that he was visibly carrying arms, was such evidence sufficient to prove the aiding and abetting as crimes? And these are precisely the three questions, Your Honours, that you presented in your 6 September order. We are not going to repeat the arguments that we presented in the appeal brief. We will show that the Trial Chamber was erroneous in their analysis of evidence. The Appeals Chamber has a duty to prevent a miscarriage of justice and must correct legal errors that are invalidating a judgement in all cases before the Tribunal. I am referring here to the Appeals Chamber judgement in the Kupreskic case especially paragraphs 127 through 227, where the Trial Chamber's findings were reversed in relation to Witness H. We have a similar situation in our case like in the Kupreskic case, especially taking into account the conflicting evidence explained in our appeal in paragraphs 1 and 2, and now I'm going to present some additional arguments. We therefore urge the Appeals Chamber to interfere by applying the same standards as it did in paragraphs 222 through 227 of the Kupreskic appeals judgement, and I would like to start with my PowerPoint presentation, page 1. And now if you look at the screens before you, in keeping with the indictment and the evidence presented by the Prosecutor, we will say that the incident at Pionirska was divided by the Prosecutor into five different stages. The first one is arrival of the Koritnik group, the second is the robbery, the third is the strip-search, the fourth is the transfer, and the fifth the events at Adem Omeragic's house. And can we now move on to slide number 2. [In English] Is everything fine with the presentation? May I continue, Your Honour? [Interpretation] I hope that you have slide number 2 on the screens before you and this slide depicts the five stages of the incident, and if you look at those, the Trial Chamber has found that Sredoje Lukic was present and that he was involved in incidents number 2 and 4, namely, the robbery and the transfer. I would like to point out that Judge Robinson presented a dissenting opinion with regard to the participation of Sredoje Lukic in the transfer. I have to say that there was a considerable time-span between the two incidents. The robbery took place about 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon, whereas the transfer took place around 11.00 in the evening. Even with such factual findings, Judge Robinson's dissenting opinion, if it had been supported by the Trial Chamber, a question would be posed: What would be the legal foundation for Sredoje Lukic's participation in the robbery alone? What I would like to point out - and I would like to refer you to the slide - the Trial Chamber concludes that Sredoje Lukic was present in the robbery based on the testimonies of four witnesses. They are VG-038, VG-18, VG-084, and Huso Kurspahic. Four of the total of nine witnesses who provided evidence and they are actually the weakest link, in our submission, in the charges brought against Sredoje Lukic. What we did not point out in our appeal brief and I would like to point out at this point is the contradiction between the findings relative to these witnesses. And if you would like to look at the first column, you will see that there is a paragraph marked for each of these witnesses. In the second column we provided all the exculpatory evidence. In the third column there is a reference to identification. And in the fourth column there is a question, and that is whether there is ample evidence to prove that Sredoje Lukic was armed. And Professor Knoops will say more about that. We believe that the Trial Chamber's conclusion from paragraphs 593 and 930 of the judgement, whereby the Trial Chamber placed Sredoje Lukic outside of the house during the robbery that was taking place in the house. Contrary to that finding, none of the four witnesses were able to establish that Sredoje Lukic was outside of the house while the robbery was taking place inside the house. VG-38, according to the Trial Chamber, only heard from other persons who Sredoje Lukic was. VG-18 and 84 allegedly heard when he presented himself and introduced himself in the house, whereas Hasib Kurspahic provided hearsay evidence nonspecific to the whereabouts of the appellant during the incident. I have to correct a word that I used on page 18 [as interpreted], line 18, Huso Kurspahic. Furthermore, I would like to point out the double standards that the Trial Chamber uses in respect of the previous jurisprudence of the Tribunal. In the Vasiljevic case, the same witness, Huso Kurspahic, was called as a witness and he testified about the same incident. He presented the same evidence. However, the Trial Chamber in the Vasiljevic case refused to accept everything that the witness stated and that was not in the statement of his father who was a survivor of the incident, Hasib Kurspahic. Completely different conclusions were reached at -- during that case. I would like to point out that it was Hasib Kurspahic, who is Huso Kurspahic's father and who survived the incident, gave an interview only 24 days after the incident and that was the first piece of evidence in this case. Again I would like to make reference to Judge May and his book on international criminal evidence and the rule on the best evidence. The significance of this evidence lies in the fact that nobody ever contradicted this evidence. It is Exhibit Number P40 and another one, P41. And in this interview Hasib Kurspahic mentioned quite a number of names, including Mitar Vasiljevic, who was convicted before this Tribunal. The Trial Chamber established that Hasib Kurspahic and Sredoje Lukic were well acquainted before the war, they knew each other well before the war. If Sredoje Lukic had indeed been involved in the incident, i.e., if he had been at the crime scene, Hasib Kurspahic would have certainly mentioned him in the interview. And, Your Honours, I now would kindly ask you to look at page 2 in our tables. That page contains the conclusions of the Trial Chamber, exculpatory material identification and the question whether the Trial Chamber found that any of the witnesses provided ample evidence or sufficient evidence that my client was indeed carrying arms during the incident. The conclusion of the Trial Chamber in paragraph 607 is again very contradictory to the conclusions of the Trial Chamber in terms of the robbery. Certain ambiguities appear which are very significant. How was it possible for somebody who did not see Sredoje Lukic but only heard of him and about him, allegedly saw him at that moment, and without any prior information about Sredoje Lukic, and there was also no voice recognition. And again, a completely different standard is applied to the testimony of Huso Kurspahic than the one applied in the Vasiljevic case. In our appeal brief you will find a more detailed elaboration of this argument, but what I would like to say is this: The evaluation of evidence by the Trial Chamber was completely erroneous. On the one hand, the Trial Chamber uses the evidence of 13-year-old boys to conclude as well as a hearsay witness, Huso Kurspahic; and on the other hand, we have credible witnesses who demonstrated that Sredoje Lukic was not present during the incident. Those witnesses are VG-13, mother of Witness VG-38, the two of them were together throughout the entire duration of the incident. VG-13's mother knew -- [In English] Mother of VG-13 knew Sredoje Lukic before the incident. [Interpretation] Whereas the son, VG-38, did not know him. The conclusion of the Trial Chamber regarding the mother was that there was no evidence to show that Sredoje Lukic was there, and on the other hand, there is credibility given to the testimony of VG-38. Another contradiction can be seen between Hasib Kurspahic's testimony, i.e., his interview, and the evidence provided by Huso Kurspahic. And in addition to that I would like to mention some other Prosecution witnesses who never mentioned Sredoje Lukic and those were VG-78, VG-101, CW-2, and last witness knew Sredoje Lukic from before the war but in her evidence she did not mention him as one of the participants in the incident. And I am saying all this in order to make reference to the standards applied in the Limaj case. In paragraph 153 of the appeals judgement it is stated that when it comes to the evaluation of identification evidence one has to take into account both evidence for and against. In addition to that I'm referring to paragraphs 39 and 40 in the Kupreskic case appeals judgement, where the Appeals Chamber found that: "A Trial Chamber must proceed with extreme caution when assessing a witness's identification of the accused." The Trial Chamber did not emphasise a single important fact that adversely affects identification evidence and thus omitted to state its reasoned opinion. I would now like to draw your attention to the screens before you with a summary of our presentation. In our appeal brief -- and again we have tried to present a reasonable alternative as to who might have been at the crime scene instead of Sredoje Lukic. This is an excerpt from the testimony of Mitar Vasiljevic. The Prosecutor clearly asks about a description of the fourth member of the group at the crime scene, and Mitar Vasiljevic clearly indicates VGD4, whereas in this case he testified that Sredoje Lukic had not been in Visegrad on that day at all. The same description was provided by a number of witnesses. VGD4 has a name and surname and they are in evidence. To date we have received no disclosure regarding any possible investigation against VGD4, although his identity is known, and although there is enough evidence that VGD4 was involved in this crime rather than Sredoje Lukic. Moreover, VGD4 is also mentioned regarding the river Drina incident. The Trial Chamber failed to even consider this important evidence. Therefore, we must point out that once again the Trial Chamber failed to provide a reasoned opinion. The question arises: How could the Trial Chamber find that it was proven beyond reasonable doubt that Sredoje Lukic was present throughout the Pionirska Street incident, considering that the role of VGD4 in this incident has never been investigated? Thank you for your attention, Your Honours, and now I'm giving the floor to my learned friend Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for giving me the floor. Thank you, Mr. Kremer, for accepting the PowerPoint presentation. Your Honours, I've put my oral submissions on paper just to assist the Chamber with the references and I can speed up my oral submissions by perhaps presenting the presentation to the Legal Officers so they can follow the oral submissions, and I can skip the references because you find in the footnotes all my references to the case law and the legal textbooks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm going to object to it being distributed, on the basis that this material is argumentative and Mr. Knoops can, in fact, argue based on his oral submissions. It has new material which is not in the brief and our quick review suggests maybe it raises new arguments that are not even in the appeal. And so I would ask that if Mr. Knoops is only concerned about references to cases --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: -- that he wants to provide to the Legal Officers, then I have no objection to you taking those out and putting them on a separate sheet. But in terms of the argument in total which goes on for about 21 pages, I think that it would be unfair at this point to add new submissions without having a full opportunity to review them and discuss them and reply to them. So I offer that as an alternative to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I have no problem with that, Your Honour. It's not a problem for me. It was just a matter of courtesy to the Court, but if the Prosecution objects, I have no problem that we just provide the references. I will show it -- it has no new arguments in it, just further substantiation of our arguments. But let's move on and I can indicate to the Chamber where the relevant references are in view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you accept how we shall proceed? This has been accepted by the Prosecution. I believe that the issue has been settled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: It was my understanding that this concerns only the PowerPoint presentation which was accepted, not the submission I just handed over. But I accept the objection of the Prosecution in terms of if the Prosecution thinks that they have too little time to prepare, it's fine with me. It's just an extensive reflection of my oral submissions and it's just there to assist the Chamber and, with all respect, I will not waste time discussing this document. I can move on with my oral arguments and present the reference in a separate document, no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you for your understanding. As regards the point at issue, I would like to thank both parties. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I will deal with the third -- with the question the Chamber asked us in a 6 September order to address. But of course, before I go into that specific question, it is to be emphasised that the precondition for answering this question the Chamber asked us to address is, of course, the positive answer to the questions, the first two questions, raised by my learned friend Mr. Cepic: Was Mr. Sredoje Lukic present at all at the crime scene; and if so, was he armed at the crime scene? And when there is no compelling or credible evidence to this extent, I quote the Appeals Chamber in Kupreskic, paragraph 226, then the criterion of "wholly erroneous" comes into play. It's actually one of the criteria of the Appeals Chamber to define what the term "wholly erroneous" actually legally means before this Court. So the question I'm going to address to the Court, of course, presupposes that the Chamber would at any point come to a positive answer of the first two questions you did find on the first slide of Mr. Cepic's presentation. Before I go into that question, Your Honours, we have to be reminded that the initial case, the initial theory of the Prosecution, was built on the assumption that Mr. Sredoje Lukic was involved, present, during all five stages you find on the first slide of Mr. Cepic's presentation. Yet, we know now that the findings of the appeals -- of the Trial Chamber which were not disputed by the Prosecution, was such that it only accepted a presence of Mr. Lukic, Sredoje, at the stages 2 and 4, namely, the robbery, stage 2; and stage 4, the transfer to Adem Omeragic's house. In order to build a case on aiding and abetting on these two subjects, of course it's important also to look at the time-frame between those stages. And when you reconstruct the case and the Trial Chamber's findings, you can deduce from these findings that at the minimum five hours elapsed between the robbery and the transfer, stage 4. And all five stages we're dealing with here dealt with almost a full day. I come to the relevance of this observation, Your Honours, in a later stage of my submissions. Now, as mentioned, the Prosecution did not dispute, it did in fact accept the finding of the Chamber that Sredoje Lukic allegedly was only involved in stage 2 and 4. And the question therefore is just to find whether aiding and abetting also to the crime of murder and inhumane acts can be based on just these two stages only on the only concrete tangible argument, the tangible physical element which is only here, namely, that Mr. Lukic was at the crime scene, first of all; and secondly, while visibly carrying arms. At the crime scene relates to the stages 2 and 4 - we come to that in a minute - and the second assumption, carrying visibly arms, relates only to the stage 2 because the Chamber accepted that at stage 4 Mr. Lukic was not found to be there in the presence of an arm, of a weapon. Now, the misrepresentation by the Chamber of these basic findings were at the basis of the miscarriage of justice the Defence alleges to be available here. And the Chamber, only relying on these two stages and the absence of any other tangible element or evidence than the mere presence while visibly carrying arms, misstated the law in accepting that it amounted to aiding and abetting to the Counts 9, 10, and 11 -- 9, 10 -- till 12, sorry. Now, let us go first to table 4, please, that's the fourth table. It's on the screen, Your Honours. Let us first look at what actually was concluded by the Chamber in relation to this first element, the crime scene. On the left side of the table you find the original testimony of the four relevant witnesses on which the findings were based by the Trial Chamber. And on the right side you find the -- what I call the distortion of that evidence by the Chamber, the -- what we call the denaturisation of the evidence by the Chamber. And at the bottom of this table you find the conclusion. Actually, none of the witnesses actually saw Mr. Sredoje Lukic in the house, which was the crime scene where the robbery took place. Even two of the witnesses were unable to distinguish between Milan and Sredoje Lukic, which also calls into question the Appeals Chamber findings in Kupreskic concerning Witness H in the paragraphs 222 till 226, in which the Chamber, as I recalled, gave a definition of the term "wholly erroneous." And at the right side of the table you find the observation -- the finding of the Chamber that Mr. Lukic was merely present "at the scene of the robbery," at the scene of the robbery. Notably, Judge Robinson in his dissenting opinion held merely that all the evidence shows is that Sredoje Lukic was present, not present at the crime or in the house where the robbery took place, without giving an exact location. That's correct -- correctly interpreted by Judge Robinson, because the evidence you see on this table was unable to pin-point Mr. Sredoje Lukic at the real crime scene, namely, the robbery inside the house. That is why criminal law doctrine uses the concept of constructive presence, that is a term introduced already by Blackstone years ago. You find also in the -- one of the US leading textbooks of Boyce and Perkins where I quoted from page 741 and the applicable case law therein. Actually, this doctrine says if the precise location of a co-accused is disputed, in other words, if it's not clear where that precise location was, you cannot without any other tangible evidence qualify that mere presence without a precise location being identified as aiding and abetting. And that is why in the -- this leading textbook, reflecting the US common law on the doctrine of aiding and abetting, they explained why the principle in the second degree should be present at the perpetration of the felony, either actually - which is here not the case because it was accepted that Mr. Sredoje Lukic was outside the crime scene, namely, the house where the robbery took place - or, in the alternative, constructively, by rendering actual and immediate assistance to the perpetrator. And this could be done, says Blackstone, with constructive presence. Now, this constructive presence doctrine consists of co-operating with the perpetrator and being so situated as to be able to aid him with a view known to the other "to ensure success in the accomplishment of the common purpose." Your Honours, to ensure success in the accomplishment of the common purpose. This implies, therefore, that being at the crime scene, not being the actual crime scene, can only be accepted as a type of aiding and abetting if that presence, apart from the identification of this precise location outside the actual crime scene, did ensure success in the accomplishment of the mission by the principal perpetrator. The evidence before us, Your Honours, nor the Trial Chamber's findings, lends support to the assumption that Mr. Sredoje Lukic's presence did ensure success in the accomplishment of the common purpose, whatever this common purpose might have been. There is no evidence of a common purpose, of a plan between the principal perpetrator and Mr. Sredoje Lukic or other people. He was not privy to any information whatsoever; it's not in the evidence. Constructive presence, therefore, cannot be accepted - that is the doctrine - in the event the accused cannot be conclusively linked to the actual crime scene and when it's unclear whether he did, in fact, ensure success in the accomplishment of the common purpose. In other words, if a robbery takes place within a certain house and somebody was outside that building without being established that such a common purpose existed, one cannot have said to have aided and abetted the robbery in question. Since the Trial Chamber did not at any point conclude to a more specific location of the alleged presence of Mr. Lukic in stage 2, the robbery, nothing can be inferred about the manner in which he allegedly assisted or contributed, et cetera. Did he keep watch? We don't know. It's not in the evidence. How was he situated towards the main perpetrator? We don't know. The door might have been closed. Was he within sight or hearing of the crime itself? It's not in the evidence. How was he -- was he simply there? Was his presence outside the house of Jusuf Memic relevant to ensure success in the accomplishment of that common purpose? We don't know the answer, Your Honours. We don't simply know it. Any of these questions are not answered in the evidence. And therefore, we cannot establish the nature, if there was any, of Sredoje Lukic's contribution, let alone whether this contribution was substantial. The quantitative standard for aiding and abetting. Since all these other scenarios cannot be reasonably excluded, one cannot accept the artificial argument of the Trial Chamber that constructive presence was the only reasonable inference. The former president of this Tribunal Professor Cassese in his textbook "International Criminal Law," the last edition, summarises the law as follows: "Mere presence may only imply aiding and abetting when such presence involves substantial encouragement to the crime on account of the authority of the onlooker, with the consequence that the perpetrator," and this is essential, Your Honours, "draws moral and psychological support or legitimatising effect from that presence." And Professor Cassese mentions as examples, for instance, "that person was superior to the perpetrator or had an important status in society or in the military." None is the case here. Mr. Sredoje Lukic was not a superior to any of the other alleged perpetrators nor had he important status in the society. We come to that point later in time. So here, Your Honours, you see the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have spoken to us at length -- Mr. Knoops, you have spoken to us at length about constructive presence which relates to the issue we are discussing. Could you give us the relevant criteria that apply to constructive presence. In what circumstances could one talk about constructive presence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: My answer to that question, Your Honour, I come to that in a minute as well, is that constructive presence can only be accepted as a foundation for aiding and abetting if the person is actually at the crime scene, meaning the actual crime scene, while that presence is accompanied with other tangible actions or by way of the authority of that person would lead to an encouragement or moral support. And Your Honours know the case law of this Tribunal. The Appeals Chamber have only accepted tacit approval, moral support, encouragement, in the event of previous statements, oral support, meaning that somebody is encouraged verbally, is encouraging the principal perpetrators verbally, and other elements. And if you look at the case law of this Court, although your Court doesn't use the term "constructive presence," but maybe it is equivalent to having a substantial effect on the activities of the principal perpetrator. Maybe it's -- it could be a equivalent, you see. And this is actually maybe table 6, just to skip time and answer the question of the President. In our table 6, Your Honour, you find a comparison of the other most relevant precedents on aiding and abetting and you see that in the other cases where aiding and abetting was accepted before this Court, there was no dispute about the physical presence of the defendant and the precise location. For instance, Aleksovski, he was present at the precise location of the forced labour of the prisoners, which prisoners had to undergo, and the location where they were used as human shields. Vasiljevic, he was armed and present at the Vilina Vlas hotel, escorted the seven persons to the bank, pointing a gun at them, and stood right behind the seven Muslim men with his gun. Also here there was no doubt about the actual presence of the defendant at the actual crime scene. Furundzija, Appeals Chamber 21 July 2000, commander of the Jokers, also different in terms of authority. He acted and continued to interrogate particular victims. His actions went beyond mere presence, but most importantly there was no dispute about these individuals being there on the actual crime scene, and therefore the step towards constructive presence was easy to take by the Court. So the precondition for constructive presence is there is no dispute as to the precise location of the defendant, the alleged co-perpetrator. If that's not in the evidence, you cannot, of course, come to the other criteria, such as practical assistance, moral encouragement, and was the alleged support substantial. Akayesu, the same. The Trial Chamber judgement, it was proven that he, in his capacity as a buergermeister, also here a different personality in terms of authority, was present during numerous incidents of sexual violence, et cetera. And finally in the Haradinaj Appeals Chamber judgement paragraphs 347, 348, where Lahi Brahimaj, the member of the KLA General Staff, also quite different in authority compared to Sredoje Lukic, was present when three witnesses were beaten. He beated himself Witness 6, he interrogated Witness 3, et cetera. Also here these five examples from previous cases before this Court on aiding and abetting clearly show that constructive presence requires an undisputed location of the alleged co-perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your explanation. I would like to tell you that you have 15 minutes left before our 30-minute break; or more precisely, you have 12 minutes left, so please do take this into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Then I move on to slide -- table number 5, please. This relates to the stage 4, the transfer. Trial Chamber accepted by majority, Judge Robinson dissenting, that Mr. Lukic was present during and participated in the transfer. And you find on table 5 the evidence which was used by the Chamber, and you see here that the end conclusion is that arms were not mentioned by the witnesses except for Witness VG-084, who gave conflicting evidence as to who had what weapon, automatic, sniper, or sniper-automatic. These two individuals here in the table were actually mixed by the witness, and that's why despite this testimony of VG-084, the Court only accepted presence of Mr. Lukic during the transfer, not presence with an arm. That is a huge difference. That means that the natural result of this analysis is, first, Lukic was merely present during the transfer, paragraph 607; he was merely placed at the scene of the crime not being the actual crime scene, paragraph 605; and no other tangible or physical acts were established on part of Mr. Lukic, other than in one stage, also conflicting evidence, stage 2, the potential presence of an arm, which arm, by the way, which gun was according to the evidence not used. In the Vasiljevic case, the Court -- the Appeals Chamber accepted aiding and abetting in this regard because this individual pointed at the victims and stood behind the victims with a gun. This is not established in the evidence in this case and this is also the reason why Judge Robinson in dissenting opinion came to the same very conclusion. Therefore, Your Honours, concluding, there are only two stages relevant for this case and only in one stage visibly carrying arms was accepted by the Chamber and these findings are not sufficient, I would say far not sufficient, for the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt to accept aiding and abetting for the Counts 9 till 12. Lastly, there are seven arguments why -- additional arguments why even if the Chamber were to accept that Mr. Sredoje Lukic was during stage 2 indeed visibly carrying arms, seven reasons why without further tangible evidence, that's the additional criterion, the question Your Honours asked us to address in your 6 September order has to be answered with a firm no. Visibly carrying arms does not amount to aiding and abetting in the circumstances of this case with this analysis in our minds. First, he was not present during all the stages. I already mentioned. The Prosecution assumes differently. Says in light of all the events that took place. Secondly, there were no physical actions entertained by the defendant with that rifle, at least it was not established in evidence, contrary to Vasiljevic Appeals Chamber. Thirdly, and maybe we can go back to table 6, which illustrates these clear differences with the other cases. Mr. Sredoje Lukic was just an ordinary policeman without rank or title, not dressed in a police uniform, by the way, and it was not proven, it was not in evidence, that he introduced himself as a police officer. He didn't say: Hey, I'm John Doe, I'm a police officer working at this police station. It's not in the evidence. He didn't wear any distinct police emblems or whatsoever. He had no authority, he was not superior to, these are all differences with the cases you find on this table 6. Four, as mentioned, no other tangible acts to amount to practical assistance or moral support, other than merely being present at the scene, whatever the scene might be. It's not again precise. Now, Your Honours, what I find striking is that the Chamber in paragraph 1.034 states that Sredoje Lukic aided and abetted the burning of Adem Omeragic's house, while in 613, it is concluded that there is no reliable evidence that Sredoje Lukic participated in setting Adem Omeragic's house on fire or shooting at the windows of Adem Omeragic's house. How can you reconcile these two paragraphs, these two findings? How can somebody aid and abet the burning of a house if there's no reliable evidence that's the same person participated in setting this house on fire? Because this is exactly what these two paragraphs read, Your Honour. How can without any tangible evidence during stage 5, criminal liability be referred. The same with the strip-search and the removal, paragraphs 594 and 596, the Court accepts that Mr. Sredoje Lukic was not involved in these activities, yet in the closing paragraph 637, it accepts that he participated in the strip-search and the removal. These are clearly contradictory findings of the Chamber which cannot support a conviction for aiding and abetting. I'll move on, sixth, the alleged acts do not amount to the qualification substantial, we already addressed this point. And I have to stress that there is no evidence that Mr. Lukic at any point used verbal encouragement or prior statements. There was no reaction and the Court in Aleksovski also already accepted that the absence of a reaction on part of an alleged aider and abettor is not sufficient for -- to sustain a conviction for aiding and abetting. Let alone that, this of course, requires that those actions specifically are directed to assist the principal perpetrator. None of this is the case. Finally seven, the threshold for mens rea is not met. Three clear contra-indications for the assumption that this was fulfilled. First, I already mentioned that the mens rea for the murders is only inferred by the Chamber from Sredoje Lukic's alleged presence during transfer, stage 4. Because if the transfer has no substantive bearing on this case, there is no conviction to sustain for the murders. In paragraph 1.033, the Chamber concludes that Mr. Lukic was present during the transfer and thereby aided and abetted the commission of the murders. Well, I don't see the evidentiary connection, the causal link, between the simple presence at the transfer and the aiding and abetting in the commission of the murder, because there's no evidence to establish that Sredoje Lukic's alleged knowledge of the murders was in evidence. And here the Appeals Chamber Vasiljevic clearly says in an analogous situation where the acts are ambiguous allowing for several reasonable inferences you cannot enter such a conviction. The time lapse already mentioned, the second contra-indication is five hours, and the third contra-indication is the contradiction already mentioned between paragraph 613 and 1.034, accepting that Mr. Sredoje Lukic was not involved in the shooting or the burning of Adem Omeragic's house. How can the requisite mens rea for murder be deduced simply for an event, the transfer that took place, more than hours before the alleged murder. And lastly, I think that after the Oric Trial Chamber judgements which was upheld in appeal on the element of mens rea for aiding and abetting, the requirements you find in our appeal brief, there are four requirements, I will not repeat them. The Appeals Chamber in Haradinaj came with a judgement on the 9th July 2010, paragraph 58, introducing or reinforcing the double intent requirement that the aider and abettor knew that his own acts assist the commission of that specific crime by the principal, and, in addition, that the aider and abettor was aware of the essential elements of the crime which was ultimately committed by the principal. All this cannot be inferred, even not by inference, from the evidence because the evidence is not saying that Mr. Sredoje Lukic was privy to information and concerted plan or the true intentions of the principal perpetrator or perpetrators. And after an analysis of all the reasonable alternative inferences above, the reasonable trier of fact could not have concluded that the -- [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: This is my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We shall now have a break for 30 minutes. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is back in session. I would like to invite the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor to submit their response, and I would like to remind you that you have one hour and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Your Honours, on 14 June 1992, Sredoje Lukic assisted Milan Lukic and a band of armed Serb men as they robbed, humiliated, and terrorised and then killed a large group of Muslims from Koritnik on Pionirska Street in Visegrad. On several occasions in the second half of 1992 and the early months of 1993, Sredoje Lukic severely beat Muslim prisoners in the Uzamnica detention camp. After having heard the evidence and listened to the arguments put forward on his behalf, the Trial Chamber properly convicted Sredoje Lukic for his crimes. Although he attempts to re-argue all of the issues that were raised at trial and fairly considered by the Trial Chamber, he fails to show that the Trial Chamber erred and his appeal should be dismissed. In responding to his arguments made today, the Prosecution will present its submissions in the following order. I will first answer the Appeals Chamber's second question. I will then address some of the other issues Sredoje Lukic raises concerning his liability for aiding and abetting the crimes at Pionirska, particularly dealing with the issue of identification. And Mr. Schuster will address his crimes at Uzamnica. The circumstances of the Pionirska Street case are -- have to be looked at in the context of a group of Muslims from Koritnik who were forced by armed Serbs to leave their town and go to Visegrad, and finally being redirected to a house on Pionirska Street in the early afternoon of June 14, 1992. It has to be looked at in the context that Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, and other armed men who were identified as Mitar Vasiljevic, Milan Susnjar, came in the later afternoon and started to rob, humiliate and then terrorise the victims, many of whom were women, children, elderly, and some babies. They were armed. They were wearing camouflage uniform. And the first act when they had an encounter with the Muslims in the Memic house was to identify themselves, both Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic, and then Milan Lukic - according to the finding of the Trial Chamber - directed the Muslims to hand over their valuables on pain of death. The robbery, the strip-searching, and the other humiliating conduct, including the taking away of three women to be raped, during the next two to three hours, all in the context of refugees fleeing, expecting to be transferred, being terrorised by four armed men led by Milan Lukic. At night Sredoje Lukic, Milan Lukic, and the same armed men returned, armed again, and with flash-lights, flash-lights because it was dark, it was 11.00 at night.
