The Muslims immediately were transferred from the Memic house to the Omeragic house which had been prepared with a fire accelerant. Our position - and the Chamber found - is that Sredoje Lukic actively participated in the transfer, helping, in the Chamber's words, to herd the victims into the execution house. Milan Lukic set fire to the house and members of the group shot at victims who attempted to escape. The Chamber found and therefore didn't convict Sredoje Lukic of committing the crime of murder because there was no evidence that he set the house on fire or shot at the victims. But the monstrous act that resulted from the actions of Milan Lukic were aided and assisted by Sredoje Lukic. There was premeditation and calculation in it and Milan Lukic and the group came together and carried it out, both in the afternoon and in the evening. The Chamber heard the evidence of the witnesses who came to testify about the events, and as I said earlier this morning, carefully assessed the evidence and properly applied the guiding legal principles, both in terms of the consideration of the evidence and in relation to identification. Sredoje Lukic's conviction for aiding and abetting is entirely reasonable and supported by the evidence. Let me deal with question number 2, because the issue of whether he was armed has been raised and I will address whether that finding is supported by the evidence. The Chamber unanimously found that Sredoje Lukic, Milan Lukic, and the other men in the Lukic group were all armed with automatic rifles, grenades, and bayonets, and wore camouflage uniforms, both in the afternoon and at night. At night Sredoje Lukic, Milan Lukic, and the others also carried military flash-lights. Sredoje Lukic was armed during the robbery in the afternoon - I refer to paragraphs 343, 583, 593, 637. VG-38 mentioned that Sredoje Lukic had an automatic weapon. VG-18 referred to an automatic rifle. Sredoje Lukic was armed at night when he assisted in herding the victims from the Memic house to the Omeragic house. It's paragraph 604, and I mention that there is not a word in the submissions of my friends opposite about paragraph 604 in their submissions this afternoon, paragraph 607 as well. VG-38 testified that he saw Sredoje Lukic with an automatic weapon at the time of the transfer - this is paragraph 419 - citing transcript 984. On cross-examination by Mr. Cepic, VG-38 confirmed that in addition to their automatic weapons, Sredoje Lukic and the other men had grenades and bayonets. That's at transcript page 984 which is footnoted in trial judgement 419. VG-84 also confirmed that the four men who returned to the Memic house to conduct the transfer included Sredoje Lukic and that they were armed. That's at trial judgement 604. The point I want to make is that the distinction that the appellant makes in this particular case about the confusion between Milan and Sredoje Lukic by witnesses 84 and 38 does not take away from the fact that Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic were armed. It does not take away from the fact that they were present at the various locations. For example, when Milan Lukic threatened - and there was an issue as to who threatened the victims prior to the robbery - ultimately the decision taken by the Trial Chamber that it was Milan Lukic, but the evidence is that Sredoje Lukic was also there. He and Milan Lukic both identified themselves to the victims. Milan Lukic then told them to give up their valuables, and at some point Sredoje Lukic, who at that point may have been identified as Milan Lukic, went outside. But the Chamber's finding based on all of the evidence as it understood it and as it accepted it, was that Milan Lukic ordered the Muslims to give up their belongings, their valuables, and he was armed and Sredoje was armed in the room when that threat was made. That presence beside Milan Lukic when the threat is -- beside or in the room with Milan Lukic at the house when the threat is made is sufficient. Now, the finding isn't specific, the legal finding, that Your Honours have asked us to deal with isn't as specific as it perhaps could have been. But the previous findings, the previous factual findings, bear-out, particularly when the references to the transcript pages are examined, bear-out that that is, in fact, the case. What Mr. Knoops would have you find is that unless there is a witness that specifically says: Mr. Sredoje Lukic pointed his gun and therefore the robbery occurred in order to justify a conviction for aiding and abetting is clearly wrong. On the facts of this case, four armed men in camouflage uniform come to an already distressed group of individuals and ask them on their arrival, within seconds -- within a short time of their arrival: Give up your valuables. And then other crimes are committed during the next two to three hours. Also, when they come back, the four of them come back together, again armed with grenades, with bayonets, and with rifles, and with flash-lights. And the inference that they all came back with weapons is easy to make even without the evidence because after the transfer of the victims from the Memic house to the Omeragic house, they were shooting. They were shooting at the people who were trying to escape. And followed by shooting of the people who had escaped in an effort to hunt them down. So the armed group was working together. There was no other purpose when they came back, because they did nothing else other than move them to the house and set it on fire, that is possible. And Sredoje Lukic being among the group assisted the group just by his presence but he did more than just be present. Mr. Knoops would have you believe this is a case of an innocent by-stander. He just happens to come along with a group of three other soldiers and stand around. Well, that's not so and the evidence shows that it's not so. Because the finding of the Trial Chamber is that he participated in the transfer, not that he was present during the transfer. And his presence and his participation is what raised his contribution to aiding and abetting. His armed presence during the day, as I've just pointed out, just given the fact that he was in the room when they were asked to give up their valuables, when the robbery began, whether he remained in the room or not for the duration of the robbery, is sufficient for aiding and abetting. The assistance is substantial because four armed men were -- at that point he is -- the evidence is that he and Milan Lukic are in the room at the house, and therefore he substantially assisted or contributed to the crime. For the murders, it's important to stress that the Chamber found Sredoje Lukic's acts and conduct during the incident as a whole contributed to the commission of the murder. Our position is that the Trial Chamber was correct to consider the totality of Sredoje Lukic's conduct that day because Milan Lukic and the group committed a series of crimes against the same Muslim victims, they robbed them, they abused them physically and mentally, they raped some of them, and ultimately they killed the vast majority of them. The Trial Chamber had considerable discretion in determining whether Sredoje Lukic's conduct that day in its totality amounted to aiding and abetting. The Appeals Chamber has confirmed repeatedly this discretionary standard. I refer you to the Brdjanin appeals judgement at paragraph 276; and the Nahimana appeal judgement paragraph 512. The Trial Chamber in this case properly exercised its discretion. Your Honours, Sredoje Lukic actively assisted in the crimes. Because as a member of this group that was committing only crimes, it wasn't there for any other reason, he came with Milan Lukic, he was in the house, he left the house, he left with the group at some point, and then they came back. His involvement was never innocent. His involvement was always criminal. And when Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic and the other men arrived on Pionirska Street in the afternoon, their criminal purpose quickly revealed itself. As I say, there were the self introductions. Milan Lukic threatening the victims while he and Sredoje were in the room fully armed. He also threatened to sever fingers and cut the throat and put a bullet in the head of anyone who withheld anything. These aren't friendly words; they're criminal words. And the criminal activity of this group is illustrated and must be taken into account in assessing the conduct of Sredoje Lukic. Sredoje Lukic was in the house while they were robbed. He was in -- he was at the house while the members of the armed group strip-searched the women and children. He was at the house when Milan Lukic removed the three women, and when the women returned, they said they had been raped and those three women all perished in the fire. His armed or visibly armed presence, as the Trial Chamber described it, as a member of the Lukic group, both inside and outside the Memic house, shows that the victims had no choice but to comply. He had an impact on whether or not the victims would give up their valuables, would submit themselves to a strip-search, or would go from the Memic house to the Omeragic house. And when combined with the threats that were being issued by Milan Lukic, on departing he told the Muslims not to leave on pain of death, indicating that they were going for food and drink. And they left, Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, and the others. And these extremely vulnerable and frightened Muslims, stripped of their last remaining valuables, which Milan Lukic put in a bag and took with him, remained in the house at the mercy of their attackers should they return. Later that night Milan Lukic returned with Sredoje Lukic and the others, just as he had promised. They were armed again, as I say, with automatic rifles, grenades, and bayonets. And they also brought flash-lights. And the flash-light reference is paragraph 354 trial transcript -- transcript 1408, and P355, transcript 1410. And other witnesses describe flash-lights and how they were used in the movement of the people from one house to the other. The Muslims were ordered to move to the nearby Omeragic house, where they would be killed. Now, as the victims left the house, Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and another soldier told them to leave their shoes behind. That's at trial judgement 359. Without their shoes, it would be much more difficult for them to escape from their executioners. The Muslims complied. Now, the flash-lights provided the light or part of the light that was used during the transfer of the Muslims in part to ensure that no one ran away. They were told to stay on the road. And the men formed an armed corridor between the Memic house and the Omeragic house and, according to the words or descriptions used by the Trial Chamber, "herded the Koritnik group to the Omeragic house," trial judgement 605, referring to trial judgement 362. And I refer you specifically to footnote 1250 and also suggest looking at trial judgement 601. During the transfer, Sredoje Lukic and other members of the armed group moved around the path between the houses, again ensuring that no one escaped. That's at trial judgement 601. The Omeragic house had been prepared for the victims. Its floor was soaked with a fire accelerant with a pungent smell, and I talked earlier today about VG-13's description that the air in the room was suffocating, causing people to choke, trial judgement 1032. Sredoje Lukic was present as a member of the armed corridor and the group assisting in the transfer of the people, and although there's no direct evidence that he was present when the house was ignited, which Mr. Knoops would have you require before he can be convicted of aiding and abetting, his presence is obvious. There are four members of the group who came to commit a crime. They all participated in moving the people to the Omeragic house. The only reasonable inference possible is that he was there when it was set on fire and he was there when the shooting took place. Now, there's no evidence that he shot and there's no evidence that he lit a match and threw it in. But that's not what's required for aiding and abetting. That's what's required for committing, and that's why Milan Lukic was convicted of committing and Sredoje Lukic was only convicted of aiding and abetting. Witnesses who managed to escape, including VG-18, described how the killers pursued them with their flash-lights to illuminate the scene. That's in trial judgement 377. Why was Sredoje Lukic's assistance during the day and evening a substantial contribution to the murder of the Muslims in the house? I will give you three reasons. There are probably many more. One, he cowed the victims into submission through his armed presence and his reputation as a local policeman; two, he reassured the fellow perpetrators by his participating alongside them in the sustained and brutal attack; and three, and perhaps most importantly, he actively helped to herd the large group of victims into the pre-prepared execution house where they were burned alive. The Chamber was correct in finding that by his acts and conduct throughout the entirety of the events Sredoje Lukic made a substantial contribution to the crime of murder for the crimes for which he was convicted. And even if you forget about what happened in the afternoon, his conduct at night is more than sufficient to justify a conviction for aiding and abetting. And Judge Robinson in his dissent I would say, with respect, was wrong to require more. Shooting victims and throwing explosives into the house equals committing, not aiding and abetting. The evidence was more than ample to show that Sredoje Lukic aided and abetted Milan Lukic's crime. He was with Milan Lukic from the beginning and through the end of this series of crimes that started in the early afternoon of June 14th, 1992. Now, before I move on to some of the other issues that Mr. Lukic has raised on appeal, this is perhaps an appropriate time to address the issue of mens rea. I want to start by pointing out or emphasising again that what Mr. Knoops did not do in his discussion of the mens rea is talk about his participation - he ignored it - his participation in the transfer. His presentation is based on the misreading of the evidence that Sredoje Lukic was there, unarmed, standing around, watching. And a fair reading of the evidence and certainly how the Trial Chamber interpreted it was that he did much more. And I won't repeat myself about -- on this. There are two findings that the Chamber makes regarding mens rea and one relates to the cruel treatment and the infliction of inhumane acts on the victims of the robbery, and in his reply brief at paragraphs 66 and 67, Sredoje Lukic suggests that the Chamber's findings are not well founded on the evidence. With respect, there was a series of crimes organised and committed by a small group. Sredoje Lukic knew the crimes against them were an assault on their human dignity or were an assault on the human dignity of the victims and would cause mental anguish as a result of their loss of their remaining valuables. He was there when Milan Lukic made the demand or the threat that they deliver up their valuables. He had the necessary mens rea for those crimes. Turning to murder. The Chamber also found that Sredoje Lukic knew that the persons whom he had helped place into and who had been locked into Adem Omeragic's house would be killed as a result of the fire when the house was set ablaze and that he also knew that his acts and conduct contributed to the commission of murder. Again, the Chamber took into account the chain of events that day. Sredoje Lukic argues that all of this could be reasonably inferred is that he assisted the people for their allegedly planned transfer of the day. This is in his appeal brief at paragraph 179. We didn't hear anything about that today, but it shows how cynical Sredoje Lukic is about his presence. There was no evidence that there was any step taken by the Milan Lukic group in the afternoon or the evening to assist in these people's transfer. On the contrary, all of the evidence points to the fact that they were there to persecute and to commit serious crimes against the victims. In fact, the Trial Chamber made an explicit finding that the alleged transfer the next day was merely a ruse to get the people to a single point. And the Chamber made extensive findings on the discriminatory atmosphere, at paragraph, in the judgement, 1027 and following. Sredoje Lukic knew that the detention of these people was illegal and nothing could justify the robbery and the humiliation of the women and children. There was no purpose in locking them in a room with carpets covered with a sticky, pungent substance. And there was -- and which functioned as a fire accelerant, by the way, other than to kill them. And his participation in the movements, in the herding of the people to the house, would have given him enough information about Milan Lukic's intention when the door was locked behind them, the smell, and then ultimately when the flame was started. Mr. Knoops says he can't aid and abet because he didn't contribute to lighting the match or he didn't contribute to shooting at the victims, but that's not the test. The test is did he contribute to murder -- did he know that murder would result? And the Trial Chamber reasonably found, based on all of the circumstances, what was happening to the victims, the smell of the house, and what had happened earlier in the day, this was a criminal act that could only result in the murder of the victims. Another factor is the organised manner in which these crimes were taking place in -- particularly the murder. The murder was at night. Murder maybe could have taken place in the afternoon, but the murder was at night, so they needed flash-lights and other light to ensure that they could do what they intended. Flash-lights were only used for one purpose: To move the people from the Memic house to the Omeragic house and to light up the people who were escaping or the windows in order to shoot, to ensure that everyone was killed. He arrived with them with a flash-light, he arrived with them armed and he participated, as he was required to do, to ensure that the operation was successful. His acts, I would submit, justify the Chamber's finding that Sredoje Lukic knew that his intended -- knew of the intended fate of the Muslims and that Milan Lukic was intending to kill them. On the basis of this evidence I would submit that the Chamber was fully entitled to find that Sredoje Lukic knew what the fate of the victims would be in the afternoon and in the evening and that his participation would facilitate their demise. He had the necessary mens rea for aiding and abetting. Now in his submissions this afternoon, Sredoje Lukic has yet again repeated arguments which call, I would submit, impermissibly for a de novo review of the evidence. He had raised all of these arguments at trial. He has again raised these arguments in his appeal brief and they were answered in the Prosecution response brief. His submissions in his appeal brief and his submissions in court add nothing to these points and provide no further assistance, I would submit, to the Appeals Chamber in its deliberations. I will give you three brief examples. First, with regard to the alleged inconsistencies of VG-38's evidence, Sredoje Lukic raised these arguments at trial, paragraphs 62 to 69, 80 to 81 of his closing brief. It was considered in the judgement at paragraphs 417, 582, 585, and 601. He repeats the same arguments at paragraphs 49, 81 to 84, 97 to 101 of his appeal brief. And they were answered at paragraphs 40 to 41, 57, 62 to 65 of the Prosecution response brief. The same applies for the alleged inconsistencies in the evidence of VG-84. He raised them, paragraphs 113 to 121, and 126 to 131 of his closing brief. It was considered in the judgement, paragraphs 403 to 407, 590, and 604. He repeats this argument at paragraphs 45 to 48 of his appeal brief, 72 to 78, and 102 to 106, and the responses of the Prosecution are found in paragraphs 35 to 39, and 66 to 67. With regard to the alleged inconsistencies of Huso Kurspahic's evidence, he raised it in paragraphs 179 to 183 of his closing brief. The Chamber considered it in its judgement, paragraphs 387 and 591. He repeats the same argument at paragraphs 53 to 57, and it's answered in paragraphs 42 to 44, and 68. The point I want to make is that much of the arguments being advanced to suggest there are identification issues, that -- are really asking the Chamber to review in detail the evidence that was led at trial and to replace the discretion of the Trial Chamber with your discretion, to put yourself in the uncomfortable position of not having seen the witnesses, not having heard the witnesses, not having heard all of the evidence and put the evidence into its proper context, a job that the Trial Chamber did well and the Appeals Chamber should not embark on unless it is absolutely necessary. And in our submission, it is not necessary in this case. I just want to deal with a couple of issues on identification. I just want to check how my time is going. I want to highlight, first of all, that the Chamber was unanimous in finding that Sredoje Lukic was present at Pionirska Street during the day and at night as a member of the Lukic group and based its findings on a variety of mutually reinforcing evidence. And the evidence isn't as weak as Mr. Knoops would suggest, or Mr. Cepic as well, when one looks at it as a whole instead of under a high-resolution microscope. Sredoje Lukic was identified by several witnesses, including VG-38, VG-18, VG-84, and as we've heard, Hasib Kurspahic. After hearing the evidence and the evidence of Hasib Kurspahic through his son, the Trial Chamber found each of these witnesses' accounts to be credible and reliable. VG-18 and VG-84 heard Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic introduce themselves after they entered the Memic house, just before they robbed the Muslim victims. Sredoje Lukic challenges this by repeating his trial argument that VG-18 and VG-84 gave differing accounts on hearing this introduction. The Chamber, as I've alluded to already, noted the differences at paragraphs 588 to 590 of its judgement and limited its findings to VG-18 and VG-84's consistent evidence, that both heard Sredoje Lukic introduce himself. And I would submit that since both witnesses said they were together when they heard this introduction, the Chamber was entitled to make this finding. It was not required - as the appellant would suggest - to determine exactly where in the room they were standing. He also argues that VG-13 and VG-38 were with VG-18 and VG-84 but did not hear the same introduction. That's in his appeal brief at paragraph 40. This argument rests on a false premise. Because VG-18 did not say that VG-13 and VG-38 were right beside her when she heard Sredoje Lukic introduce himself. Instead, she simply acknowledged that VG-13 and VG-38 were in the same room at the Memic house at the time. Simply being in the same room does not mean that the witnesses would have seen and heard exactly the same things, especially when it is a crowded room. Both witnesses identified Milan and Sredoje Lukic as being present. That fact eliminates the possibility that only one of the accused was present at the Pionirska Street crimes. And that's how the Chamber resolved any difficulty with identification where the person said: I heard both introduce themselves. I saw both of them. And so on, where there was a -- they limit their findings to the presence but not taking into account the evidence of the acts and conduct of the accused but their presence was noted. Hasib Kurspahic personally knew Milan [sic] Lukic. He identified him as one of the perpetrators at Pionirska Street. Hasib had told his son Huso five or six times that Sredoje Lukic was one of the perpetrators. That's at transcript page 928. Hasib Kurspahic was on good terms with Sredoje Lukic prior to the fire which supports the Chamber's reliance on his recognition of Sredoje Lukic at Pionirska Street. The Chamber's cautious and reasonable findings in relation to the identification witnesses are found at the -- in the judgement at paragraphs 586 to 591, and subsequently. Moreover, it is significant that as a local policeman, Sredoje Lukic was well-known by at least ten of the victims who died. Those victims identified him to the survivors, that's the evidence of VG-38, it's in the evidence of VG-18 and VG-84, during the events before they were murdered. As VG-84 explained on cross-examination when asked how he knew it was Sredoje Lukic, he said: "... Two men came into the house, Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic. There was one elderly man and all of my neighbours and friends who were in the house knew him, and 20 to 25 per cent of them knew Sredoje Lukic who was allegedly a policeman. I was a child at the time, so I didn't know him [...] "Q. [...] So you say that 20 to 25 per cent of your neighbours who were in the Memic house with you knew Sredoje Lukic? "A. Yes. Both of them. Both Sredoje and Milan. I'm telling you how it was roughly. I don't know the details. I was just under 14. I wasn't checking who knew them, but between 20 to 25 per cent of those who were in the house knew the two men who came into the room -- or, rather, the three men, because the third one remained in the corridor. "Q. Why would you have believed your neighbours that this was in fact Sredoje Lukic? "A. Well, why wouldn't they believe us?" I think there's a mistake there. "This was not a town of a million. Some 10.000 people inhabited it. It was a small town." I think he's speaking of Visegrad. VG-84's common sense explanation was credited by the Chamber at paragraph 590. Sredoje Lukic also disputes the Chamber's findings that victims who perished at Pionirska Street identified Sredoje Lukic to the witnesses who survived. Again, his argument rests on a false premise. In fact, the witnesses that he cites in support of his argument all stated that they heard from other victims that Sredoje Lukic was present. For example, Sredoje Lukic asserts at paragraph 12 of his reply brief that VG-101 never mentioned Sredoje Lukic. In fact, VG-101 said she was told by others that Sredoje Lukic was at the Memic house along with Milan Lukic. Yet Sredoje Lukic did not cross-examine her on the statement that she had given in Exhibit 1D36 at page 4. Sredoje Lukic also argues that VG-101 said that there was never any discussion about the identity of the four perpetrators. In fact - and that's at his reply brief at paragraph 13 - in fact, when she was asked about who the perpetrators were she answered: "Yes. A man was saying -- they were all saying that they knew them. We all knew who those men were and what they were." The Chamber validly took account that the victims knew Sredoje Lukic and identified him to the survivors who came to testify. Now, what is the evidence of Sredoje Lukic during the transfer? The Chamber was particularly careful in assessing the evidence showing that Sredoje Lukic was present and participating in the transfer of the victims to the Omeragic house. Take the Trial Chamber's treatment of VG-38's evidence, for example. VG-38 described how Sredoje and Milan, along with Mitar Vasiljevic and Milan Susnjar, carried out the transfer. The perpetrators moved about the path, which was between 20 to 30 metres, during the transfer. This is at judgement paragraph 601. Although the Chamber found that VG-38 did not know Milan and Sredoje Lukic prior to 14 June 1992, other members of the Koritnik group who did know the Lukics had identified both of them to VG-13 [sic] during the afternoon's events at the Memic house when the lighting conditions were better. Furthermore, VG-38 knew Mitar Vasiljevic and Milan Susnjar by sight, and so was able to distinguish them from Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic, as set out in the Prosecution response brief. The Chamber took a cautious approach, not relying on VG-38 with respect to Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic's precise actions, but found that VG-38's evidence established that both Lukics were present during the transfer. VG-38's account that Sredoje Lukic's involvement in the transfer is consistent with and confirmed by the accounts of Hasib Kurspahic and VG-84. Hasib Kurspahic, as I've said previously, knew Sredoje Lukic well. He recognised him as one of the men carrying out the transfer at night. That's at judgement paragraph 605. He explained to his son Huso how the Lukic group stood in a row between the houses and escorted the Koritnik group to the Omeragic house, judgement paragraph 362. VG-84 also stated that Sredoje and Milan Lukic returned to the Memic house in the evening and were armed and present during the transfer, judgement paragraph 604. And further direct evidence supporting the Chamber's finding is set out in the Prosecution brief at paragraph 23 and in paragraphs 597 to 607 of the judgement. There is a lot of evidence that was considered and having heard the evidence and heard the witnesses, the Chamber was entitled to rely on their mutually reinforcing accounts. Sredoje Lukic was present, armed, and participated in the transfer of the victims that resulted in the crimes, crime of murder, at Pionirska Street. And this fact was found by the majority. The one thing I want to emphasise is Sredoje Lukic's presence during the period of the crimes in Pionirska Street was found unanimously by the Chamber. Judge Robinson only dissented on whether his conduct amounted to a substantial contribution for aiding and abetting, i.e., did he participate in the transfer. Sredoje Lukic also challenges -- or Sredoje Lukic's challenges to identification of Sredoje Lukic during the transfer are further answered by the contextual evidence, which supports the Chamber's finding of his participation. VG-84 said: "There was light in front of the house. They had flash-lights. Everything had been prepared in advance." Speaking of the Omeragic house, that's at transcript page 1285. At the Omeragic house, the floor had been soaked with fire accelerant which fuelled the flames when Milan Lukic set the fire. That's at paragraphs 559 to 560. The group was armed and organised and prepared. In this context, there is no innocent explanation for Sredoje Lukic's presence at Pionirska Street. Although he wasn't wearing a uniform, Sredoje Lukic had been a policeman and he may have been a policeman at the time, paragraph 1090. Also, Sredoje Lukic had been a policeman in Visegrad before the war and continued to serve in this capacity during the war, is the finding. He should have been preventing crimes. Instead, he chose to assist the crimes of Milan Lukic, his cousin, and others to transfer the people to a pre-prepared place for their execution. Sredoje Lukic's arguments today and in his brief do not demonstrate that the Chamber breached it discretion in finding him guilty of the crimes and they did -- made no mistake in finding that the deceased witnesses who knew Sredoje Lukic as a policeman or as a neighbour told the surviving witnesses of his identity. The Chamber heard the accounts of the survivors who escaped, carefully assessed their evidence, and properly applied the guiding legal principles, both in relation to identification and in determining that Sredoje Lukic knowingly made a substantial contribution to the horrific crimes committed against the Muslim victims at Pionirska Street. The Chamber's conviction of Sredoje Lukic for aiding and abetting is entirely reasonable and supported by the evidence and, in our submission, his appeal or appeals on these conviction should be dismissed. Subject to any questions you might have, I will turn the podium over to Mr. Schuster.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHUSTER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will make -- I will be making the Prosecution's submission in relation to Uzamnica. I will respond to the points raised by Mr. Cepic early on and I will also answer your questions that you raised at the beginning of this hearing in the course of my presentation. Your Honours, the Chamber correctly found that Sredoje Lukic came to the Uzamnica camp on a number of occasions and savagely assaulted the Muslim prisoners that were kept there under deplorable living conditions. Sredoje would beat and kick them with his fists, with a rifle, with wooden stakes, and one time with a long pole. Three witnesses identified Sredoje Lukic as their assailant. Two of them, Dervisevic and Kustura, knew Sredoje Lukic from before the war because he was a police officer. One of them, Dervisevic, would even testify that he saw him at the local bar in Visegrad. The reference is transcript 1999. The third witness, Berberovic, learned from the others at the camp of Sredoje Lukic's identity as one of the men who would come and beat him. In this regard, Your Honours, I refer you again to para 196 of the Rukundo appeal judgement, where the Appeal Chamber held that a Chamber can rely on the evidence of witnesses who learned of the identity of their tormentor through other persons. While there were some inconsistencies in the witness's evidence, which can be expected given the circumstances of their detention, all of these were taken into account by the Trial Chamber. What Sredoje Lukic attempts to do is to artificially isolate the evidence, evidence that the Chamber considered as a whole. By doing this, Sredoje Lukic also just repeats his trial submissions. They were all taken into account by the Trial Chamber, but he doesn't show any error. For the details on his submissions, I point Your Honours to our brief. I only refer to three points which Sredoje Lukic's Defence mentioned this morning and the questions that Your Honours have raised. The issue of Dervisevic's and Kustura's prior statements was explicitly discussed by the Chamber. Kustura's prior statement of November 1994 is a three-page document in which Kustura speaks about events spanning two years. Now, he didn't mention Sredoje Lukic, but again it's a three-page document talking about three years of events. On the contrary, he gave about a hundred pages of viva voce testimony before the Trial Chamber and he confirmed repeatedly to the Trial Chamber that it was Sredoje Lukic as one of the people beating him. Again, I've already mentioned this, Kustura knew him before the war as a policeman. The Chamber also discussed Kustura's explanation why he had not mentioned Sredoje Lukic earlier. It expressly acknowledged at 834 of the trial judgement that he did not explain this omission to its satisfaction, but it reasonably considered Kustura's repeated oral testimony tested under cross-examination that Sredoje Lukic was always coming with Milan Lukic as corroboration of the other witnesses' evidence. Likewise, the Chamber noted in paragraph 1--813 of the judgement that Dervisevic did not mention Sredoje Lukic in some of his prior statements, but it also recalled that he confirmed repeatedly in court that he was certain that he was beaten by him. That's 813 of the judgement. As I've mentioned before, Dervisevic knew Sredoje Lukic before the war as a policeman. In addition, in a statement taken in 2008 he did confirm that he was beaten by Sredoje Lukic. That's P111. Your Honours, the Appeals Chamber has confirmed many times that it is up to the trier of fact to resolve differences between a witness testimony and prior statements. I refer Your Honour in this regard to the Renzaho appeal judgement, where the Appeals Chamber recalled that the Trial Chamber has the discretion to accept a witness's evidence notwithstanding inconsistencies between the evidence and his prior statements. By doing that, the Trial Chamber who in this case saw all those witnesses in court was best placed to assess their evidence and the Chamber has seen the three witnesses who confirmed that Sredoje Lukic was at Uzamnica camp beating people. At this point, I'd briefly interject about the photo-board issues that Your Honours have raised earlier. As matters stand, it is unclear whether the photo-boards shown to Witness Berberovic contains Sredoje Lukic's photo. The Chamber found that it was most probably not in the photo spread. That's at 838 of the judgement. It is also unclear whatever happened to the photo-boards. While this is unfortunate, this whole issue was discussed at trial and the Trial Chamber took explicit notice of that. 805 of the judgement. And it noted that in this situation it could not assess something that was not in evidence before it. This fact can also not be utilised at this stage, on appeal, to undermine the Chamber's findings. But in any case, it is hardly exculpatory. The Chamber mainly relied on Dervisevic and Kustura when finding that Sredoje Lukic was at the camp and to Berberovic in corroboration. Coming to the third point, one witness, VG-25, the 92 quater witness never saw Sredoje Lukic at the camp. That's his statement. But the Chamber addressed the statement and it found that it was easily explained by the different periods of detention among the various detainees testifying before the Trial Chamber. VG-25 only became an inmate in the camp at the end of November 1992, but Witness Berberovic testified that he saw Sredoje Lukic four or five times after his arrest in August 1992, a long time before November --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHUSTER
utterances.text: While Dervisevic stated that he was beaten by Sredoje Lukic in July or August, the later months, or at the end of 1993. Kustura also testified that one of the beatings took place at the end of October, again, before November when VG-25 became an inmate. And the Chamber considered precisely this, as it was required to do, at paragraph 834. This also ties into your other question. Your Honours asked whether the question of Milan Lukic's detention raised in his sixth ground of appeal has any impact on the appeal of Sredoje Lukic. The answer is no. Milan Lukic raised a question about his whereabouts in 1993. There's evidence that he was indeed in prison for parts of that year after late March; however, this does not affect the reliability of the witnesses. The Chamber was aware of the fact that the detainees did not have calendars or writing material to write on and they could not precisely pin-point the date and time of each and every beating and sighting. That is at 830 of the trial judgement. In addition, one witness, Dervisevic, testified that Lukic was away at some point during his detention because he was held in custody. Again this aligns with Milan Lukic's alleged imprisonment or indeed imprisonment in 1993. For this reason, the Chamber correctly found that minor inconsistencies in the witnesses' evidence on when Milan Lukic was present were harmless and did not distract from their convincing testimony. Your Honours, this issue has also been litigated before you in Rule 115 proceedings in relation to Milan Lukic and we submit that the same considerations there apply to the witnesses' evidence in relation to Sredoje Lukic's whereabouts. Your Honours, the Chamber addressed all the evidence raised by Sredoje Lukic at trial. It is expected that there will be certain discrepancies between eye-witness testimonies, and the Appeals Chamber has accepted that a Trial Chamber can reasonably accept parts of a witness testimony while rejecting others. That's Kupreskic Appeals Chamber paragraph 33. The Chamber did its duty to carefully review the evidence. In light of this assessment, Sredoje Lukic's challenges to his presence at Uzamnica and the beatings he committed there should be rejected. Your Honours, Sredoje Lukic was one of the perpetrators at Uzamnica. He was there at least several times brutally assaulting helpless victims. His challenges to his convictions should be dismissed. Your Honours, this concludes the Prosecution's appeal unless you have any questions I would be happy to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I would like to invite the counsel of Sredoje Lukic to present its case in reply, and I shall remind you that you have 30 minutes for doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will try to be expeditious and Mr. Knoops will continue after me. First of all, I want to emphasise that the Prosecution responded to our appeal as if they were speaking before the Trial Chamber in final arguments, not before the Appeals Chamber. They also presented certain assumptions and arguments that the Trial Chamber did not accept, whereas we invoked the relevant paragraphs in the judgement and other evidence. My learned friend Mr. Schuster in his arguments considering the Uzamnica camp are the first thing I wanted to be addressed falling under ground 6 of Sredoje Lukic's appeal. We firmly believe that there is a good substantiation -- [In English] Just clarification for the transcript regarding to the ground 6(E) and ground 6(F) of Milan Lukic's appeal, we stay on position that it has a strong impact regarding to our position because in the light of testimony of Adem Berberovic and Islam Kustura before the Trial Chamber that Sredoje Lukic and Milan Lukic came together to Uzamnica camp, it is not possible if Milan Lukic was at that time in detention unit in Belgrade, 400 kilometres away from Visegrad and camp Uzamnica. So this is the potential impact of Milan Lukic's appeal, ground number 6, for our case. Regarding to other witnesses who testified for that incident, I have to remind my learned friend Mr. Schuster that on the page 124, lines 24 and 25, he said that it is unclear about photo-spreads, are they shown are not to Adem Berberovic. I have to recall the testimony of the chief of investigation department in this case, Mr. Ib Jul Hansen, who testified in the trial and clearly explained that no photo of Sredoje Lukic were used for identification procedure. I will refer you to paragraph 252 of our appeal. Furthermore, VG-25 knew very well Sredoje Lukic before the incident and he was very clear that he did not see Sredoje Lukic in Uzamnica camp. So there is no positive identification of Sredoje Lukic in that incident. Regarding to Pionirska Street incident, as I said, my learned friend repeated arguments from the trial. On our tables we clearly presented conclusions of the Trial Chamber and findings for each of those witnesses, of four witnesses on which evidence the Trial Chamber explained and actually found presence of Sredoje Lukic in the incidents. We are on position that those testimonies are not credible and they are in a huge contradiction. Just one example. Only two witnesses who knew Sredoje Lukic prior to that incidents were VG-13 and Hasib Kurspahic. Both of them are credible for the Trial Chamber, but none of them provided evidence that Sredoje Lukic was present in that incident. This is in complete contradiction with the testimony of the son, VG-38, who just heard that Sredoje Lukic allegedly was there. It is completely illogical that in one hand you have a testimony of the mother, VG-13, who knew Sredoje Lukic prior to that incident and who did not see Sredoje Lukic in that incident, instead of the testimony of VG-38 who allegedly heard from other persons that Sredoje Lukic was there. Also, there is a huge contradiction in the testimony of Huso Kurspahic, which source of information was his late father Hasib Kurspahic. The only source of information is statement -- that interview which I quoted of Hasib Kurspahic given just 24 days after the incident. Huso Kurspahic as professional policeman had opportunity for three years to take his father to any police station even if he had a new information for potential statement before the police. So the only source is that I quoted and it is unreasonable to conclude that the testimony of Huso Kurspahic is wider than the explanation provided by Mr. Hasib Kurspahic in that interview. I would just kindly ask you to -- to review our tables and to review our -- our appeal brief, where we quoted so many discrepancies regarding to main factual findings. Thank you very much for your attention and I kindly ask Professor Knoops to continue with our presentation. Thank you very much one more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, I will raise five arguments, five responses, to the Prosecution response. First, the argument of an alleged de novo trial, de novo appeal. Even when arguments are raised during a trial session in the first instance, the case law of this Court actually obliges the Appeals Chamber to review the same materials in the event of eye-witness identification under difficult circumstances, paragraph 39 of the Appeals Chamber Kupreskic judgement, denoting for extreme caution, I quote from it, paragraph 39; and the duty to provide the reasoned opinion which is absent in the case of Sredoje Lukic by the Trial Chamber. And then the Appeals Chamber in paragraph 40 goes on to set forth that eye-witness identification in the event it is unreasonable or renders a conviction unsafe and the potential for that should be reviewed by the Appeals Chamber. And it mentions seven options, paragraph 40, under which inconsistent or inaccurate testimony about the defendant's physical characteristics at the time of the event which equally counts, I say, for certain objects allegedly in the possession of a defendant, such as an alleged weapon. And the sixth option mentioned by the Appeals Chamber in the Kupreskic case which calls for a review in its totality of the evidence when it's not compelling or credible or a serious doubt is the existence of irreconcilable witness testimony, which is clearly shown by the Defence in its tables. So with all due respect for the submissions of my learned friends from the Prosecution, we are not asking for a de novo appeal. This is just simply an application of the principles which were previously adopted by the Appeals Chamber. Now, for instance, VG-084, which is repeatedly called upon by the Prosecution, the 13-year-old boy you find also mention in the table, what did the Trial Chamber actually say about that? Paragraph 490, which is also quoted by the Prosecution. No weight on his evidence as to specific acts of Mr. Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic. I repeat, no weight on his evidence as to specific acts. He was disqualified in that respect and he was also disqualified by being not in a position to see Sredoje Lukic as he introduced himself, only he allegedly heard someone introducing that person as Sredoje Lukic. Now, I ask you, an introduction without seeing that person, is that a proper identification of the exact identity? Is it not possible that the name of that person is misused? So without a proper identification, a mere introduction, hearing that somebody's introduced as "I'm John Doe," cannot be accepted in a court of law as an introduction, I quote the Prosecution, that both identified themselves. This is wrong, this is not a wrong way -- this is not a way of identifying a person. The introduction itself, therefore, is incomplete. And therefore, if we are dealing with these types of evidence without a direct eye-witness identification at all, it's totally justified that the Defence asks the Chamber to review the evidence also in part on the facts of the case. Now, actually the Prosecution is doing what it blames the Defence to do. The Prosecution asked actually for a de novo trial. Because the Prosecution uses the alleged facts from the stages 1, 3, and 5 for which materially Mr. Lukic is acquitted, not formally, but the Court didn't accept any credible evidence for those stages 1, 3, and 5. Now, the Prosecution is using still alleged activities from those stages to say to the Court: Well, you see, you know, the totality of the events, including the stages 2 and 4, should lead to the conclusion that there was aiding and abetting. Now, this is clearly outside the scope of the Prosecution's appeal because the Prosecution appealed only on two alleged legal errors and no errors of fact. It didn't say in its brief that the Chamber entered into a miscarriage of justice invalidating the judgement by saying that the Chamber erroneously did not accept credible evidence for the stages 1, 3, and 5. So the Prosecution has no right anymore, has forfeited that right, to use that alleged evidence, that trial evidence, the transcripts from those stages, relating to those stages, to substantiate a case which was found by the Court to include only the stages 2 and 4. This is the other way around what the Prosecution is doing. Thirdly, the five stages, if you look at those stages, Your Honour, stage 1, VG-115 was found not credible. No weight on any alleged identification of Mr. Milan Lukic or Sredoje Lukic herding the persons. It is simply not accepted by the Court that those defendants herded the people in the first stage, paragraph 579. Then the second stage, alleged robbery. The Court in 593 only found that Mr. Sredoje Lukic was armed and present. No participation. The Prosecution misstates the evidence accepted by the Court by qualifying being armed and present as participating, but that is not what the Chamber says in 593, no participation. Then stage 3, the strip-search and removal -- we can still use the PowerPoint, of course, as Your Honours know -- but maybe it's just a repetition. The third stage which is used by the Prosecution in terms of the totality of the events, the strip-search and removal of the women, paragraph 594, not involved, no participation, VG-013, 108 and 1084, para 596, Milan Lukic removed the women, no word of Sredoje Lukic. So Prosecution cannot use any arguments from that stage. The transfer. Prosecution says, well, if somebody is not able to distinguish those two defendants he can still identify or say something about the arms. Well, this is really the question whether this is permissible under the Kupreskic guide-lines which denotes in case of conflicting evidence extreme caution and a reasoned opinion, which is not to be found in the judgement. Therefore, only a 13-year-old boy, VG-084, was the only one in this stage of the transfer who said something about arms, confusing the defendants and the arms, automatic rifle or a sniper. So there were two mistakes, two identification mistakes made, by a 13-year-old boy. Still his evidence was to be found credible to sustain that Mr. Lukic was armed in the fourth stage, the transfer stage. This is really a big question for the Court whether this is acceptable under the Kupreskic guide-lines in the paragraph 39, 40, 222 to 226, where it discredits Witness H and the same arguments. Prosecution says Mr. Lukic was in the house while the robbery took place. This is simply not in the evidence. Mr. Lukic was not in the house, paragraph 593 of the Chamber, a finding which was not disputed by the Prosecution in appeal. It has no right to re-open that discretion because it didn't appeal those findings. Then the last stage finding, setting fire -- setting the house on fire, shooting, Prosecution said even when not present it could still amount to a form of participation. That's the way I understand the argument of the Prosecution. The Chamber did not even held that Mr. Sredoje Lukic was present in the fifth stage. Paragraph 609, VG-013, no weight that witness for the court. Paragraph 610, VG-038, not satisfied that he saw Sredoje Lukic in the fifth phase. So how can we even take into account this fifth phase in the totality of the events when this is the findings of the Chamber which are again not disputed by the Prosecution. Then my fourth argument which relates to the response of the Prosecution on the element of substantial, the quantitative requirement for aiding and abetting. The Prosecution has had three arguments: Armed presence, reputation as a local policeman, and three, "he reassured his fellow perpetrators by participating alongside them." What type of reassurance this should have been other than merely passively there because that's the only inference from the evidence. It would then amount to a form of passive contribution. Well, this is not acceptable under the case law unless it is accompanied with verbal encouragement, while silent approval also - according to the case law of the Control Council Acts after World War II cited by Judge Cassese in his textbook "International Criminal Law," the second edition, page 215 - silent approval is not sufficient to sustain a type of aiding and abetting. That should be accompanied by either verbal encouragements or other tangible activities of that person to accept the qualification of the Prosecution that somebody is reassured, the principal perpetrators. Reputation of a policeman I already addressed. Nor in evidence is that Mr. Lukic had a form of authority and the mere introduction without proper identification cannot sustain the evidence that somebody was at the crime scene. Finally, Your Honours, you asked me during my presentation, Mr. President, please could you give a definition of constructive presence. You remember the question. I have to be honest to you, I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, I can finish in five minutes, Mr. President. Thank you very much. Well, maybe it's something for the textbook in the future, the definition of constructive presence. It's not to be found in Perkins and Boyce, I can assure you. When I prepared this case, and I tried to find all of the textbooks, Perkins and Boyce, this was one of my books I used for my own university degree, it is not here. There is case law. But of course it will be and has to be determined on a case-by-case basis. But I believe firmly when you look at the underlying rationale of constructive presence, it's all about somebody really being there. And in Furundzija, very interesting, the Appeals Chamber Furundzija accepted aiding and abetting because the two defendants were "in full view of each other." You have to -- I can give you the quotation. I think it's in -- I can give you the paragraph -- maybe Mr. Cepic there. I did prepare it -- yes, but it's in the Appeals Chamber judgement. In Furundzija Appeals Chamber judgement you find the observation of the Appeals Judges that the defendants, including the defendant who was accused for aiding and abetting, were in full view of each other or with full view of each other. This actually, I think, underlines this principle rationale for -- this precondition for constructive presence. And in the Vasiljevic Appeals Chamber decision, albeit in the context of intent in paragraph 129 and 130, you find the eight indicia the Chamber gave for the reason why they thought Mr. Vasiljevic was an aider and an abettor. And I advise you, if that's necessary, to look into those indicia. Then you -- I think you cannot other than conclude that these indicia are not here. We can maybe invent them or we can think about them like the Prosecution, but they are simply not in the evidence. Thank you very much. It's paragraph 120 of the Furundzija Appeals Chamber decision, 21 July 2000, paragraph 120: "When -- where the act of one accused contributes to the purpose of the other, and both acted simultaneously," first requirement, "in the same place," you see the degree of geographical location and the relevance thereof, "and within full view of each other, over a prolonged period of time, the argument that there was no common purpose is plainly unsustainable." But to the contrary, Mr. President, here you find the answer of constructive presence. Acting simultaneously, in the same place, with full view of each other, over a prolonged period of time. These are the minimum requirements, I would say, for aiding and abetting in terms of constructive presence. So the answer you asked me is maybe to be found in the Furundzija Appeals Chamber decision paragraph 120. And we can say a lot about this case but one thing is not in the evidence, during the robbery the two defendants alleged to be present there were not, I quote, "within full view of each other," because Mr. Sredoje Lukic was outside the crime scene, outside the house. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Knoops. It is now time to conclude today's hearing. If the parties have no comments or questions to make, I believe this hearing can be adjourned. Do you have any comments or questions? I don't see any. We shall convene tomorrow at 10.00 in the same courtroom to hear the remaining presentations of the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have been advised of the fact that this hearing will be held in Courtroom III. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of September, 2011, at 10.00 a.m.
